And he shall dwell in that city, until he stand before the congregation for judgment, and until the death of the high priest that shall be in those days: then shall the slayer return, and come unto his own city, and unto his own house, unto the city from whence he fled.” Hebrew text Joshua 20:4–6: וְנָ֞ס אֶל־אַחַ֣ת ׀ מֵהֶעָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֗לֶּה וְעָמַד֙ פֶּ֚תַח שַׁ֣עַר הָעִ֔יר וְדִבֶּ֛ר בְּאָזְנֵ֛י זִקְנֵ֥י הָעִֽיר־הַהִ֖יא אֶת־דְּבָרָ֑יו וְאָסְפ֨וּ אֹתֹ֤ו הָעִ֙ירָה֙ אֲלֵיהֶ֔ם וְנָתְנוּ־לֹ֥ו מָקֹ֖ום וְיָשַׁ֥ב עִמָּֽם׃ וְכִ֨י יִרְדֹּ֜ף גֹּאֵ֤ל הַדָּם֙ אַֽחֲרָ֔יו וְלֹֽא־יַסְגִּ֥רוּ אֶת־הָרֹצֵ֖חַ בְּיָדֹ֑ו כִּ֤י בִבְלִי־דַ֙עַת֙ הִכָּ֣ה אֶת־רֵעֵ֔הוּ וְלֹֽא־שֹׂנֵ֥א ה֛וּא לֹ֖ו מִתְּמֹ֥ול שִׁלְשֹֽׁום׃ וְיָשַׁ֣ב ׀ בָּעִ֣יר הַהִ֗יא עַד־עָמְדֹ֞ו לִפְנֵ֤י הָֽעֵדָה֙ לַמִּשְׁפָּ֔ט עַד־מֹות֙ הַכֹּהֵ֣ן הַגָּדֹ֔ול אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִהְיֶ֖ה בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֑ם אָ֣ז ׀ יָשׁ֣וּב הָרֹוצֵ֗חַ וּבָ֤א אֶל־עִירֹו֙ וְאֶל־בֵּיתֹ֔ו אֶל־הָעִ֖יר אֲשֶׁר־נָ֥ס מִשָּֽׁם׃ [… 20:4–6 as in the KJV: the slayer states his case to the elders at the gate, is not handed to the avenger, and stays until trial and the death of the high priest.] Old Greek translation Joshua 20:3 and 20:7, the verses either side of the gap: Φυγαδευτήριον τῷ φονευτῇ τῷ πατάξαντι ψυχὴν ἀκουσίως· καὶ ἔσονται ὑμῖν αἱ πόλεις φυγαδευτήριον, καὶ οὐκ ἀποθανεῖται ὁ φονευτὴς ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀγχιστεύοντος τὸ αἷμα, ἕως ἂν καταστῇ· ἐναντίον τῆς συναγωγῆς εἰς κρίσιν. Καὶ διέστειλε τὴν Κάδης ἐν τῇ Γαλιλαίᾳ ἐν τῷ ὄρει τῷ Νεφθαλὶ, καὶ Συχὲμ ἐν τῷ ὄρει τῷ Ἐφραὶμ, καὶ τὴν πόλιν Ἀρβὸκ, αὕτη ἐστὶ Χεβρὼν, ἐν τῷ ὄρει τῷ Ἰούδα. [… the Greek page runs from verse 3 straight to verse 7: no gate, no elders, no mention of the high priest’s death in the Greek of this chapter. Verse 3 and verse 9 do end with “until he stand before the congregation for judgment”.] Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/JOS20.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/20/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS20.htm.

record.title: Jephthah “buried in one of the cities of Gilead” (Judges 12:7) — the Greek has “in his city Galaad”
record.summary: The KJV puts Jephthah's burial “in one of the cities of Gilead”. The Hebrew text uses cities of Gilead. The old Greek translation instead has his city, Galaad.
record.text: KJV Judges 12:7: “And Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then died Jephthah the Gileadite, and was buried in one of the cities of Gilead.” Hebrew text Judges 12:7: וַיִּשְׁפֹּ֥ט יִפְתָּ֛ח אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל שֵׁ֣שׁ שָׁנִ֑ים וַיָּ֗מָת יִפְתָּח֙ הַגִּלְעָדִ֔י וַיִּקָּבֵ֖ר בְּעָרֵ֥י גִלְעָֽד׃ פ [… and Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in the cities of Gilead (plural).] Old Greek translation Judges 12:7: Καὶ ἔκρινεν Ἰεφθάε τὸν Ἰσραὴλ ἓξ ἔτη· καὶ ἀπέθανεν Ἰεφθάε ὁ Γαλααδίτης, καὶ ἐτάφη ἐν πόλει αὐτοῦ Γαλαάδ. [… and Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his city Galaad (singular, with “his”).] Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/JDG12.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/12/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG12.htm.
record.reasoning: The wording contrasts plural cities with one city and the added his. The KJV includes “one of” when rendering the Hebrew plural.

record.title: Micah pays the Levite “by the year” (Judges 17:10) — the Greek has “a day”
record.summary: Judges 17:10 in the KJV offers the Levite ten shekels of silver “by the year”. The old Greek translation gives ten of silver for a day. The Hebrew text uses a phrase involving days.
record.text: KJV Judges 17:10: “And Micah said unto him, Dwell with me, and be unto me a father and a priest, and I will give thee ten shekels of silver by the year, and a suit of apparel, and thy victuals. So the Levite went in.” Hebrew text Judges 17:10: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ לֹ֨ו מִיכָ֜ה שְׁבָ֣ה עִמָּדִ֗י וֶֽהְיֵה־לִי֮ לְאָ֣ב וּלְכֹהֵן֒ וְאָנֹכִ֨י אֶֽתֶּן־לְךָ֜ עֲשֶׂ֤רֶת כֶּ֙סֶף֙ לַיָּמִ֔ים וְעֵ֥רֶךְ בְּגָדִ֖ים וּמִחְיָתֶ֑ךָ וַיֵּ֖לֶךְ הַלֵּוִֽי׃ [… ten (of) silver for the days, and an order of garments, and your keep.] Old Greek translation Judges 17:10: Καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ Μιχαίας, κάθου μετʼ ἐμοῦ, καὶ γίνου μοι εἰς πατέρα καὶ εἰς ἱερέα, καὶ ἐγὼ δώσω σοι δέκα ἀργυρίου εἰς ἡμέραν, καὶ στολὴν ἱματίων, καὶ τὰ πρὸς ζωήν σου. [… ten (of) silver for a day, and a robe of garments, and what is for your living.] Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/JDG17.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/17/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG17.htm.
record.reasoning: The Hebrew days phrase can express a year's span, as the KJV renders it. The Greek gives a daily interval, producing a different pay period.
record.scope: The finding concerns only the year/day contrast at Judges 17:10. The unstated silver unit in Hebrew and Greek is not another finding. The record does not decide the intended interval, establish an exact wage or claim the Greek misread its source. record.title: Micah’s “house of gods” (Judges 17:5) — the Greek has “house of God”
record.summary: Judges 17:5 in the KJV says Micah “had an house of gods”. The old Greek translation uses a singular phrase, house of God.
record.text: KJV Judges 17:5: “And the man Micah had an house of gods, and made an ephod, and teraphim, and consecrated one of his sons, who became his priest.” Hebrew text Judges 17:5: וְהָאִ֣ישׁ מִיכָ֔ה לֹ֖ו בֵּ֣ית אֱלֹהִ֑ים וַיַּ֤עַשׂ אֵפֹוד֙ וּתְרָפִ֔ים וַיְמַלֵּ֗א אֶת־יַ֤ד אַחַד֙ מִבָּנָ֔יו וַיְהִי־לֹ֖ו לְכֹהֵֽן׃ [… Micah had a house of ’elohim; and he made an ephod and teraphim …] Old Greek translation Judges 17:5: Καὶ ὁ οἶκος Μιχαία αὐτῷ οἶκος Θεοῦ· καὶ ἐποίησεν ἐφὼδ καὶ θαραφίν· καὶ ἐπλήρωσε τὴν χεῖρα ἀπὸ ἑνὸς υἱῶν αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐγένετο αὐτῷ εἰς ἱερέα. [… Micah’s house was to him a house of God; and he made an ephod and teraphim …] Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/JDG17.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/17/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG17.htm.
record.reasoning: The Hebrew text's word has a plural form but can refer to one God or several gods. Its grammar alone does not settle Micah's intended deity.
record.scope: The finding concerns the KJV/Greek wording at Judges 17:5, not two established conflicting facts. It does not decide the author's intended reading or call the KJV wrong. record.title: “The LORD hath testified against me” (Ruth 1:21) — the Greek has “the Lord humbled me”
record.summary: At Ruth 1:21, the KJV has Naomi say “the Lord hath testified against me”. The old Greek translation says the Lord humbled her.
record.text: KJV Ruth 1:21: “I went out full and the Lord hath brought me home again empty: why then call ye me Naomi, seeing the Lord hath testified against me, and the Almighty hath afflicted me?” Hebrew text Ruth 1:21: אֲנִי֙ מְלֵאָ֣ה הָלַ֔כְתִּי וְרֵיקָ֖ם הֱשִׁיבַ֣נִי יְהוָ֑ה לָ֣מָּה תִקְרֶ֤אנָה לִי֙ נָעֳמִ֔י וַֽיהוָה֙ עָ֣נָה בִ֔י וְשַׁדַּ֖י הֵ֥רַֽע לִֽי׃ [… and the Lord has ‘anah in me (answered/testified against me, or afflicted me) …] Old Greek translation Ruth 1:21: Ἐγὼ πλήρης ἐπορεύθην, καὶ κενὴν ἀπέστρεψέ με ὁ Κύριος· καὶ ἱνατί καλεῖτέ με Νωεμὶν, καὶ Κύριος ἐταπείνωσέ με, καὶ ὁ ἱκανὸς ἐκάκωσέ με; [… and the Lord has humbled me, and the Sufficient One has treated me ill.] Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/RUT01.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/8/1/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/RUT01.htm.
record.reasoning: Testifying against someone suggests a courtroom scene; humbling someone does not carry that same image. Naomi's next clause also describes harm. These printed renderings differ without establishing which Hebrew sense is correct.
record.scope: This comparison concerns Ruth 1:21 only. No dictionary was opened to settle the Hebrew word's meaning. The finding is limited to the KJV and the named Greek edition, without claiming a Hebrew translation error. record.title: Ezra 7:12 (the king’s greeting) — “perfect peace” against “let the word and the answer be completed”
record.summary: Ezra 7:12 in the KJV greets Ezra with “perfect peace, and at such a time”. The old Greek translation asks that the word and answer be completed. The source language of this verse is Aramaic.
record.text: KJV Ezra 7:12: “Artaxerxes, king of kings, unto Ezra the priest, a scribe of the law of the God of heaven, perfect peace, and at such a time.” Aramaic text Ezra 7:12: אַ֨רְתַּחְשַׁ֔סְתְּא מֶ֖לֶךְ מַלְכַיָּ֑א לְעֶזְרָ֣א כָ֠הֲנָא סָפַ֨ר דָּתָ֜א דִּֽי־אֱלָ֧הּ שְׁמַיָּ֛א גְּמִ֖יר וּכְעֶֽנֶת׃ [Aramaic rendering: complete, and now.] Old Greek translation Ezra 7:12: Ἀρθασασθὰ βασιλεὺς βασιλέων Ἔσδρᾳ γραμματεῖ νόμου Κυρίου τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ· τετελέσθω λόγος καὶ ἡ ἀπόκρισις. [Greek rendering: let a word and the answer be completed.]
record.reasoning: The KJV presents a greeting of peace, while this Greek wording presents a request for completion. The Aramaic text does not include a word for peace.
record.scope: This finding concerns the greeting/completion wording at Ezra 7:12 only. The difficult Aramaic phrase does not establish a KJV translation error here. This record does not prove the meaning of a Persian official formula. The cited Greek edition groups Ezra and Nehemiah under Esdras. record.title: Ezra 7:26 (the king’s penalties) — “banishment” against “chastisement”
record.summary: Ezra 7:26 in the KJV lists death, banishment, loss of goods and imprisonment. The old Greek translation uses chastisement, or corrective punishment, as its second item. Both lists have four items.
record.text: KJV Ezra 7:26: “And whosoever will not do the law of thy God, and the law of the king, let judgment be executed speedily upon him, whether it be unto death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment.” Aramaic text Ezra 7:26: וְכָל־דִּי־לָא֩ לֶהֱוֵ֨א עָבֵ֜ד דָּתָ֣א דִֽי־אֱלָהָ֗ךְ וְדָתָא֙ דִּ֣י מַלְכָּ֔א אָסְפַּ֕רְנָא דִּינָ֕ה לֶהֱוֵ֥א מִתְעֲבֵ֖ד מִנֵּ֑הּ הֵ֤ן לְמֹות֙ הֵ֣ן [לִשְׁרֹשׁוּ כ] (לִשְׁרֹשִׁ֔י ק) הֵן־לַעֲנָ֥שׁ נִכְסִ֖ין וְלֶאֱסוּרִֽין׃  פ [Aramaic: the text marks separate forms to write and to read; their meaning is not settled here.] Old Greek translation Ezra 7:26: Καὶ πὰς ὃς ἂν μὴ ᾖ ποιῶν νόμον τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ νόμον τοῦ βασιλέως ἑτοίμως, τὸ κρίμα ἔσται γινόμενον ἐξ αὐτοῦ, ἐάν τε εἰς θάνατον, ἐάν τε εἰς παιδείαν, ἐάν τε εἰς ζημίαν τοῦ βίου. ἐάν τε εἰς παράδοσιν. [Greek rendering: to death, to chastisement, to loss of property, to delivery.]
record.reasoning: The comparison is banishment versus corrective punishment in the second position. The Greek does not add an extra penalty.
record.scope: The finding concerns only the second penalty at Ezra 7:26. The fourth items are outside this comparison. No KJV error or settled meaning of the Aramaic word in Persian official usage is claimed. The cited Greek edition groups Ezra and Nehemiah under Esdras. record.title: Ezra 9:7 (Ezra’s prayer) — “our priests” against “our children”
record.summary: At Ezra 9:7, the KJV and Hebrew text name “our kings, and our priests” among those handed over. The old Greek translation instead names our sons.
record.text: KJV Ezra 9:7: “Since the days of our fathers have we been in a great trespass unto this day; and for our iniquities have we, our kings, and our priests, been delivered into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, and to a spoil, and to confusion of face, as it is this day.” Hebrew text Ezra 9:7: מִימֵ֣י אֲבֹתֵ֗ינוּ אֲנַ֙חְנוּ֙ בְּאַשְׁמָ֣ה גְדֹלָ֔ה עַ֖ד הַיֹּ֣ום הַזֶּ֑ה וּבַעֲוֹנֹתֵ֡ינוּ נִתַּ֡נּוּ אֲנַחְנוּ֩ מְלָכֵ֨ינוּ כֹהֲנֵ֜ינוּ בְּיַ֣ד ׀ מַלְכֵ֣י הָאֲרָצֹ֗ות בַּחֶ֜רֶב בַּשְּׁבִ֧י וּבַבִּזָּ֛ה וּבְבֹ֥שֶׁת פָּנִ֖ים כְּהַיֹּ֥ום הַזֶּֽה׃ [Hebrew rendering: our priests.] Old Greek translation Ezra 9:7: Ἀπὸ ἡμερῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν ἐσμὲν ἐν πλημμελείᾳ μεγάλῃ ἕως τῆς ἡμέρας ταύτης· καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἀνομίαις ἡμῶν παρεδόθημεν ἡμεῖς καὶ οἱ βασιλεῖς ἡμῶν καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ ἡμῶν ἐν χειρὶ βασιλέων τῶν ἐθνῶν ἐν ῥομφαίᾳ, καὶ ἐν αἰχμαλωσίᾳ, καιὶ ἐν διαρπαγῇ, καὶ ἐν αἰσχύνῃ προσώπου ἡμῶν, ὡς ἡ ἡμέρα αὕτη. [Greek rendering: our kings and our sons.]
record.reasoning: Priests and sons describe people differently, but these groups need not be wholly separate.

record.title: Ezra 9:11 (the prophets’ words on the land) — “an unclean land” against “a land subject to disturbance by removal”
record.summary: At Ezra 9:11, the KJV and Hebrew text describe an unclean land and the people's impurity. The old Greek translation uses wording about a land being moved and removal.
record.text: KJV Ezra 9:11: “Which thou hast commanded by thy servants the prophets, saying, The land, unto which ye go to possess it, is an unclean land with the filthiness of the people of the lands, with their abominations, which have filled it from one end to another with their uncleanness.” Hebrew text Ezra 9:11: אֲשֶׁ֣ר צִוִּ֗יתָ בְּיַ֨ד עֲבָדֶ֣יךָ הַנְּבִיאִים֮ לֵאמֹר֒ הָאָ֗רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֨ר אַתֶּ֤ם בָּאִים֙ לְרִשְׁתָּ֔הּ אֶ֤רֶץ נִדָּה֙ הִ֔יא בְּנִדַּ֖ת עַמֵּ֣י הָאֲרָצֹ֑ות בְּתֹועֲבֹֽתֵיהֶ֗ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר מִלְא֛וּהָ מִפֶּ֥ה אֶל־פֶּ֖ה בְּטֻמְאָתָֽם׃ [Hebrew rendering: land of impurity, in the impurity of the peoples.] Old Greek translation Ezra 9:11: ἃς ἔδωκας ἡμῖν ἐν χειρὶ δούλων σου τῶν προφητῶν, λέγων, ἡ γῆ εἰς ἣν εἰσπορεύεσθε κληρονομῆσαι αὐτὴν, γῆ μετακινουμένη ἐστὶν ἐν μετακινήσει λαῶν τῶν ἐθνῶν ἐν μακρύμμασιν αὐτῶν, ὧν ἔπλησαν αὐτὴν ἀπὸ στόματος ἐπὶ στόμα ἐν ἀκαθαρσίαις αὐτῶν. [Greek rendering: being moved, removal.]
record.reasoning: Unclean and removal are the printed wording contrast. The Greek wording is not shown to rule out impurity as a figurative meaning.

record.title: Ezra 9:13–14 — “punished us less than our iniquities deserve” and a question of anger, against “there is none such as our God” and a plea
record.summary: At Ezra 9:13, the KJV says God has “punished us less than our iniquities deserve”. Verse 14 asks whether God would be angry if they sinned again. The old Greek translation describes God as unequalled, lightening their wrongs, then pleads that God not be angry.
record.text: KJV Ezra 9:13–14: “And after all that is come upon us for our evil deeds, and for our great trespass, seeing that thou our God hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve, and hast given us such deliverance as this; Should we again break thy commandments, and join in affinity with the people of these abominations? wouldest not thou be angry with us till thou hadst consumed us, so that there should be no remnant nor escaping?” Hebrew text Ezra 9:13–14: וְאַֽחֲרֵי֙ כָּל־הַבָּ֣א עָלֵ֔ינוּ בְּמַעֲשֵׂ֙ינוּ֙ הָרָעִ֔ים וּבְאַשְׁמָתֵ֖נוּ הַגְּדֹלָ֑ה כִּ֣י ׀ אַתָּ֣ה אֱלֹהֵ֗ינוּ חָשַׂ֤כְתָּֽ לְמַ֙טָּה֙ מֵֽעֲוֹנֵ֔נוּ וְנָתַ֥תָּה לָּ֛נוּ פְּלֵיטָ֖ה כָּזֹֽאת׃ הֲנָשׁוּב֙ לְהָפֵ֣ר מִצְוֹתֶ֔יךָ וּ֨לְהִתְחַתֵּ֔ן בְּעַמֵּ֥י הַתֹּעֵבֹ֖ות הָאֵ֑לֶּה הֲלֹ֤וא תֶֽאֱנַף־בָּ֙נוּ֙ עַד־כַּלֵּ֔ה לְאֵ֥ין שְׁאֵרִ֖ית וּפְלֵיטָֽה׃  פ [Hebrew rendering: 13, you held back beneath our wrongs; 14, will you not be angry with us.] Old Greek translation Ezra 9:13–14: Καὶ μετὰ πᾶν τὸ ἐρχόμενον ἐφʼ ἡμᾶς ἐν ποιήμασιν ἡμῶν τοῖς πονηροῖς καὶ ἐν πλημμελείᾳ ἡμῶν τῇ μεγάλῃ, ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ὡς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὅτι ἐκούφισας ἡμῶν τὰς ἀνομίας, καὶ ἔδωκας ἡμῖν σωτηρίαν· Ὅτι ἐπεστρέψαμεν διασκεδάσαι ἐντολάς σου, καὶ ἐπιγαμβρεῦσαι τοῖς λαοῖς τῶν γαιῶν· μὴ παροξυνθῇς ἐν ἡμῖν ἕως συντελείας, τοῦ μὴ εἶναι ἐγκατάλειμμα καὶ διασωζόμενον. [Greek rendering: 13, there is none like our God, for you lightened our wrongs. 14, do not be angry with us.]
record.reasoning: The KJV joins a statement about lighter punishment with a question about anger. This Greek edition includes the fuller statement about God and frames the anger clause as a plea.
record.scope: The finding concerns Ezra 9:13 and Ezra 9:14 only. The question and plea may reflect choices in translation. This record does not decide Ezra's intended meaning or claim a KJV error. record.title: Nehemiah 5:5 (the complaint of the poor) — “other men have our lands” against “our fields belong to the honourable”
record.summary: At Nehemiah 5:5, the KJV says “other men have our lands and vineyards”. The Hebrew text names others. The old Greek translation calls them honourable people.
record.text: KJV Nehemiah 5:5: “Yet now our flesh is as the flesh of our brethren, our children as their children: and, lo, we bring into bondage our sons and our daughters to be servants, and some of our daughters are brought unto bondage already: neither is it in our power to redeem them; for other men have our lands and vineyards.” Hebrew text Nehemiah 5:5: וְעַתָּ֗ה כִּבְשַׂ֤ר אַחֵ֙ינוּ֙ בְּשָׂרֵ֔נוּ כִּבְנֵיהֶ֖ם בָּנֵ֑ינוּ וְהִנֵּ֣ה אֲנַ֣חְנוּ כֹ֠בְשִׁים אֶת־בָּנֵ֨ינוּ וְאֶת־בְּנֹתֵ֜ינוּ לַעֲבָדִ֗ים וְיֵ֨שׁ מִבְּנֹתֵ֤ינוּ נִכְבָּשֹׁות֙ וְאֵ֣ין לְאֵ֣ל יָדֵ֔נוּ וּשְׂדֹתֵ֥ינוּ וּכְרָמֵ֖ינוּ לַאֲחֵרִֽים׃ [Hebrew rendering: to others.] Old Greek translation Nehemiah 5:5: Καὶ νῦν ὡς σὰρξ ἀδελφῶν ἡμῶν, σὰρξ ἡμῶν· ὡς υἱοὶ αὐτῶν, υἱοὶ ἡμῶν· καὶ ἰδοὺ ἡμεῖς καταδυναστεύομεν τοὺς υἱοὺς ἡμῶν καὶ τὰς θυγατέρας ἡμῶν εἰς δούλους, καὶ εἰσὶν ἀπὸ θυγατέρων ἡμῶν καταδυναστευόμεναι, καὶ οὐκ ἔστι δύναμις χειρῶν ἡμῶν, καὶ ἀγροὶ ἡμῶν καὶ ἀμπελῶνες ἡμῶν τοῖς ἐντίμοις. [Greek rendering: to the honoured, or honourable.]
record.reasoning: Others leaves the group unnamed; honourable describes its standing. That wording does not identify particular officials or explain their motives.

record.title: Nehemiah 5:11 — “also the hundredth part of the money” against “from the money … bring out for yourselves”
record.summary: At Nehemiah 5:11, the KJV asks for lands to be restored. It also names a hundredth part of money, grain, wine and oil. The Hebrew text includes the hundredth wording. The old Greek translation gives no hundredth fraction.
record.text: KJV Nehemiah 5:11: “Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil, that ye exact of them.” Hebrew text Nehemiah 5:11: הָשִׁיבוּ֩ נָ֨א לָהֶ֜ם כְּהַיֹּ֗ום שְׂדֹתֵיהֶ֛ם כַּרְמֵיהֶ֥ם זֵיתֵיהֶ֖ם וּבָתֵּיהֶ֑ם וּמְאַ֨ת הַכֶּ֤סֶף וְהַדָּגָן֙ הַתִּירֹ֣ושׁ וְהַיִּצְהָ֔ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר אַתֶּ֖ם נֹשִׁ֥ים בָּהֶֽם׃ [Hebrew rendering: and the hundredth of the silver.] Old Greek translation Nehemiah 5:11: Ἐπιστρέψατε δὴ αὐτοῖς ὡς σήμερον ἀγροὺς αὐτῶν καὶ ἀμπελῶνας αὐτῶν καὶ ἐλαιῶνας αὐτῶν καὶ οἰκίας αὐτῶν, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀργυρίου τὸν σῖτον καὶ τὸν οἶνον καὶ τὸ ἔλαιον ἐξενέγκατε ἑαυτοῖς. [Greek rendering: and from the silver, bring out for yourselves the grain and the wine and the oil.]
record.reasoning: The narrow difference is a stated fraction in the KJV that this Greek edition does not print. It does not establish grain bought with money or another financial arrangement.

record.title: Nehemiah 5:14, 18 — “the bread of the governor” against “provision extorted” and “the bread of extortion”
record.summary: At Nehemiah 5:14 and 5:18, the KJV says Nehemiah did not take “the bread of the governor”. The Hebrew text names the governor too. The old Greek translation uses force at 5:14 and bread of force or extortion at 5:18.
record.text: KJV Nehemiah 5:14, 18: “Moreover from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year even unto the two and thirtieth year of Artaxerxes the king, that is, twelve years, I and my brethren have not eaten the bread of the governor. Now that which was prepared for me daily was one ox and six choice sheep; also fowls were prepared for me, and once in ten days store of all sorts of wine: yet for all this required not I the bread of the governor, because the bondage was heavy upon this people.” Hebrew text Nehemiah 5:14, 18: גַּ֞ם מִיֹּ֣ום ׀ אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּ֣ה אֹתִ֗י לִהְיֹ֣ות פֶּחָם֮ בְּאֶ֣רֶץ יְהוּדָה֒ מִשְּׁנַ֣ת עֶשְׂרִ֗ים וְ֠עַד שְׁנַ֨ת שְׁלֹשִׁ֤ים וּשְׁתַּ֙יִם֙ לְאַרְתַּחְשַׁ֣סְתְּא הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ שָׁנִ֖ים שְׁתֵּ֣ים עֶשְׂרֵ֑ה אֲנִ֣י וְאַחַ֔י לֶ֥חֶם הַפֶּ֖חָה לֹ֥א אָכַֽלְתִּי׃ וַאֲשֶׁר֩ הָיָ֨ה נַעֲשֶׂ֜ה לְיֹ֣ום אֶחָ֗ד שֹׁ֣ור אֶחָ֞ד צֹ֠אן שֵׁשׁ־בְּרֻרֹ֤ות וְצִפֳּרִים֙ נַֽעֲשׂוּ־לִ֔י וּבֵ֨ין עֲשֶׂ֧רֶת יָמִ֛ים בְּכָל־יַ֖יִן לְהַרְבֵּ֑ה וְעִם־זֶ֗ה לֶ֤חֶם הַפֶּחָה֙ לֹ֣א בִקַּ֔שְׁתִּי כִּֽי־כָֽבְדָ֥ה הָעֲבֹדָ֖ה עַל־הָעָ֥ם הַזֶּֽה׃ [Hebrew rendering: bread of the governor, in 14 and 18.] Old Greek translation Nehemiah 5:14, 18: Ἀπὸ ἡμέρας ἧς ἐνετείλατό μοι εἶναι εἰς ἄρχοντα αὐτῶν ἐν γῇ Ἰούδα, ἀπὸ ἔτους εἰκοστοῦ καὶ ἕως ἔτους τριακοστοῦ καὶ δευτέρου τῷ Ἀρθασασθὰ ἔτη δώδεκα, ἐγὼ καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοί μου βίαν αὐτῶν οὐκ ἔφαγον. Καὶ ἦν γινόμενον εἰς ἡμέραν μίαν μόσχος εἷς, καὶ πρόβατα ἓξ ἐκλεκτὰ καὶ χίμαρος ἐγίνοντό μοι· καὶ ἀναμέσον δέκα ἡμερῶν ἐν πᾶσιν οἶνος τῷ πλήθει· καὶ σὺν τούτοις ἄρτους τῆς βίας οὐκ ἐζήτησα, ὅτι βαρεῖα ἡ δουλεία ἐπὶ τὸν λαὸν τοῦτον. [Greek rendering: 14, I did not eat their force. 18, I did not seek the bread of force.]
record.reasoning: The KJV names the governor's office and its allowance. The Greek wording describes force or harsh demands. Its verse 5:15 gives nearby context about earlier rulers burdening the people.

record.title: Nehemiah 5:18 (Nehemiah’s table) — “fowls” against “a goat”
record.summary: At Nehemiah 5:18, the KJV lists one ox, six choice sheep and fowls for the daily meal. The Hebrew text has birds. The old Greek translation has a goat in their place.
record.text: KJV Nehemiah 5:18: “Now that which was prepared for me daily was one ox and six choice sheep; also fowls were prepared for me, and once in ten days store of all sorts of wine: yet for all this required not I the bread of the governor, because the bondage was heavy upon this people.” Hebrew text Nehemiah 5:18: וַאֲשֶׁר֩ הָיָ֨ה נַעֲשֶׂ֜ה לְיֹ֣ום אֶחָ֗ד שֹׁ֣ור אֶחָ֞ד צֹ֠אן שֵׁשׁ־בְּרֻרֹ֤ות וְצִפֳּרִים֙ נַֽעֲשׂוּ־לִ֔י וּבֵ֨ין עֲשֶׂ֧רֶת יָמִ֛ים בְּכָל־יַ֖יִן לְהַרְבֵּ֑ה וְעִם־זֶ֗ה לֶ֤חֶם הַפֶּחָה֙ לֹ֣א בִקַּ֔שְׁתִּי כִּֽי־כָֽבְדָ֥ה הָעֲבֹדָ֖ה עַל־הָעָ֥ם הַזֶּֽה׃ [Hebrew rendering: one bull, six choice sheep, and birds.] Old Greek translation Nehemiah 5:18: Καὶ ἦν γινόμενον εἰς ἡμέραν μίαν μόσχος εἷς, καὶ πρόβατα ἓξ ἐκλεκτὰ καὶ χίμαρος ἐγίνοντό μοι· καὶ ἀναμέσον δέκα ἡμερῶν ἐν πᾶσιν οἶνος τῷ πλήθει· καὶ σὺν τούτοις ἄρτους τῆς βίας οὐκ ἐζήτησα, ὅτι βαρεῖα ἡ δουλεία ἐπὶ τὸν λαὸν τοῦτον. [Greek rendering: one calf, six choice sheep and a kid-goat.]
record.reasoning: The finding is birds versus a goat. The separate ox/calf wording is outside this comparison.

record.title: Nehemiah 13:25 — “or for yourselves” is not in the Greek
record.summary: At Nehemiah 13:25, the KJV forbids taking foreign daughters for the men's sons “or for yourselves”. The Hebrew text includes that ending. The old Greek translation ends with the sons.
record.text: KJV Nehemiah 13:25: “And I contended with them, and cursed them, and smote certain of them, and plucked off their hair, and made them swear by God, saying, Ye shall not give your daughters unto their sons, nor take their daughters unto your sons, or for yourselves.” Hebrew text Nehemiah 13:25: וָאָרִ֤יב עִמָּם֙ וָאֲקַֽלְלֵ֔ם וָאַכֶּ֥ה מֵהֶ֛ם אֲנָשִׁ֖ים וָֽאֶמְרְטֵ֑ם וָאַשְׁבִּיעֵ֣ם בֵּֽאלֹהִ֗ים אִם־תִּתְּנ֤וּ בְנֹֽתֵיכֶם֙ לִבְנֵיהֶ֔ם וְאִם־תִּשְׂאוּ֙ מִבְּנֹ֣תֵיהֶ֔ם לִבְנֵיכֶ֖ם וְלָכֶֽם׃ [Hebrew rendering: for your sons or for you.] Old Greek translation Nehemiah 13:25: Καὶ ἐμαχεσάμην μετʼ αὐτῶν, καὶ καταρασάμην αὐτούς· καὶ ἐπάταξα ἐν αὐτοῖς ἄνδρας, καὶ ἐμαδάρωσα αὐτοὺς, καὶ ὤρκισα αὐτοὺς ἐν τῷ Θεῷ, ἐὰν δῶτε τὰς θυγατέρας ὑμῶν τοῖς υἱοῖς αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐὰν λάβητε ἀπὸ τῶν θυγατέρων αὐτῶν τοῖς υἱοῖς ὑμῶν. record.title: God Named in Five Greek Passages of Esther
record.summary: The old Greek translation names God in five places where the KJV and Hebrew text do not. Mordecai tells Esther to fear God at 2:20 and call on the Lord at 4:8. At 6:1, the Lord removes the king’s sleep. At 6:13, Haman hears that a living God is with Mordecai. At Greek 5:1e, God changes the king’s spirit to gentleness; the paired KJV passage is 5:2. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV’s Esther finds no God, gods or Lord, in any letter case.
record.text: KJV Esther 6:1: “On that night could not the king sleep” Hebrew text: בַּלַּ֣יְלָה הַה֔וּא נָדְדָ֖ה שְׁנַ֣ת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ [in that night the sleep of the king fled]. Old Greek translation: Ὁ δε Κύριος ἀπέστησε τὸν ὕπνον ἀπὸ τοὺ βασιλέως τὴν νύκτα ἐκείνην [but the Lord removed sleep from the king that night]. KJV Esther 2:20: “for Esther did the commandment of Mordecai, like as when she was brought up with him” Hebrew: וְאֶת־מַאֲמַ֤ר מָרְדֳּכַי֙ אֶסְתֵּ֣ר עֹשָׂ֔ה [and the command of Mordecai Esther did]. Greek: οὕτως γὰρ ἐνετείλατο αὐτῇ Μαρδοχαῖος, φοβεῖσθαι τὸν Θεὸν, καὶ ποιεῖν τὰ προστάγματα αὐτοῦ [for so Mardochaeus commanded her, to fear God and to do his commandments]. KJV Esther 4:8: “to make supplication unto him, and to make request before him for her people” Hebrew: וּלְבַקֵּ֥שׁ מִלְּפָנָ֖יו עַל־עַמָּֽהּ [and to make request before him for her people], the last words of the verse. Greek, continuing after the matching words: ἐπικάλεσαι τὸν Κύριον, καὶ λάλησον τῷ βασιλεῖ περὶ ἡμῶν, ῥύσαι ἡμᾶς ἐκ θανάτου. [call upon the Lord, and speak to the king about us, to deliver us from death]. KJV Esther 6:13: “thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him” Hebrew: כִּֽי־נָפֹ֥ול תִּפֹּ֖ול לְפָנָֽיו [but falling thou shalt fall before him], the last words of the verse. Greek: καὶ οὐ μὴ δύνῃ αὐτὸν ἀμύνασθαι, ὅτι Θεὸς ζῶν μετʼ αὐτοῦ. [and thou shalt not be able to withstand him, because a living God is with him]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/6/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/4/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG06.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG02.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG04.htm. KJV Esther 5:2: “she obtained favour in his sight” Hebrew text Esther 5:2: נָשְׂאָ֥ה חֵ֖ן בְּעֵינָ֑יו [she carried favour in his eyes]. Old Greek translation Esther 5:1e: Καὶ μετέβαλεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ βασιλέως εἰς πραύτητα, καὶ ἀγωνιάσας ἀνεπήδησεν ἀπὸ τοῦ θρόνου αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀνέλαβεν αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τὰς ἀγκάλας αὐτοῦ, μέχρις οὗ κατέστη· καὶ παρεκάλει αὐτὴν λόγοις εἰρηνικοῖς [And God changed the spirit of the king to gentleness, and in alarm he leapt from his throne and took her in his arms until she stood, and comforted her with peaceful words]. record.title: The Greek adds oath phrases at Song of Solomon 5:8 and 8:4
record.summary: Song of Solomon 5:8 and 8:4 appeal to Jerusalem's daughters. The KJV gives no basis for these oaths. The old Greek translation adds powers and forces of the field at 5:8. It adds forces of the field at 8:4.
record.text: KJV Song of Solomon 5:8: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.” Hebrew text 5:8: הִשְׁבַּ֥עְתִּי אֶתְכֶ֖ם בְּנֹ֣ות יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם אִֽם־תִּמְצְאוּ֙ אֶת־דֹּודִ֔י מַה־תַּגִּ֣ידוּ לֹ֔ו שֶׁחֹולַ֥ת אַהֲבָ֖ה אָֽנִי׃ Old Greek translation 5:8: Ὥρκισα ὑμᾶς θυγατέρες Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐν ταῖς δυνάμεσι καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἰσχύσεσι τοῦ ἀγροῦ· ἐὰν εὕρητε τὸν ἀδελφιδόν μου, τί ἀπαγγείλητε αὐτῷ; ὅτι τετρωμένη ἀγάπης ἐγώ εἰμι. The English version of the old Greek translation (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/SNG05.htm) prints: “I have charged you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and the virtues of the field: if ye should find my kinsman, what are ye to say to him? That I am wounded with love.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/22/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/SNG05.htm. KJV Song of Solomon 8:4: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please.” Hebrew text 8:4: הִשְׁבַּ֥עְתִּי אֶתְכֶ֖ם בְּנֹ֣ות יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם מַה־תָּעִ֧ירוּ ׀ וּֽמַה־תְּעֹֽרְר֛וּ אֶת־הָאַהֲבָ֖ה עַ֥ד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּֽץ׃ Old Greek translation 8:4: Ὥρκισα ὑμᾶς θυγατέρες Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐν ταῖς ἰσχύσεσι τοῦ ἀγροῦ· ἐὰν ἐγείρητε καὶ ἐὰν ἐξεγείρητε τὴν ἀγάπην ἕως ἂν θελήσῃ. record.title: Jehu paying tribute to Shalmaneser III (Black Obelisk)
record.summary: The Black Obelisk caption lists tribute from Jehu, son of Omri. He is usually identified with the king in 2 Kings 9–10. Those chapters describe Jehu ending Ahab's house and Hazael taking Israel's eastern lands. They do not report this tribute. A separate Assyrian account places the tribute in Shalmaneser III's eighteenth year, usually dated to 841 BCE.
record.text: KJV 2 Kings 10:11: “So Jehu slew all that remained of the house of Ahab in Jezreel, and all his great men, and his kinsfolks, and his priests, until he left him none remaining.”
record.reasoning: The caption lists silver, gold, gold vessels, lead, staves and javelins. The separate account of the king's deeds names tribute from Tyre, Sidon and Jehu after fighting Hazael. These are two distinct passages in Luckenbill's edition. The usual reading treats son of Omri as a label for the kingdom, not proof of Jehu's descent. The compared Kings account instead has Jehu destroy Ahab's house.
record.scope: The date of about 841 BCE applies to the reported tribute, not the making of the obelisk. The identification of Jehu and the kingdom-label reading remain usual interpretations. They do not prove a family link to Omri. The silence claim concerns only the compared account in 2 Kings 9–10. Its silence does not disprove the tribute. The cited Assyrian passages do not describe Jehu's coup. The later museum article checks the older translation; no new reading of the ancient signs is claimed.

record.title: Esarhaddon and Manasseh of Judah
record.summary: Esarhaddon's palace-building list names Manasseh king of Judah among rulers required to send materials. This demand suggests that Judah was under Assyrian rule. It is an inference from the list. In 2 Kings 21:1–2, Manasseh begins ruling at twelve, reigns fifty-five years and does evil. In 2 Chronicles 33:11–13, Assyrians take him to Babylon. The account says he humbles himself and returns to Jerusalem.
record.text: KJV 2 Chronicles 33:11: “Wherefore the Lord brought upon them the captains of the host of the king of Assyria, which took Manasseh among the thorns, and bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon.”
record.reasoning: The list begins with Baal of Tyre, Manasseh of Judah, Kaushgabri of Edom and Musuri of Moab. Rogers's translation and the later translation in Sources describe the demand and transport of building materials. The list does not mention Manasseh's capture, journey to Babylon or return. That silence neither proves nor disproves the Chronicles account. Kings and Chronicles report different details; this comparison does not rank their reliability.
record.scope: Chronicles does not name the Assyrian king who takes Manasseh. This record does not identify him as Esarhaddon. The quotation uses the packaged KJV's among the thorns; no alternative word meaning is established. The claim about Assyrian control rests on an inference from the demand for materials. The later translation is a check on Rogers, not a fresh reading of the tablet.

record.title: Merodach-baladan and Hezekiah
record.summary: Kings and Isaiah describe a Babylonian king sending letters and a gift after hearing that Hezekiah had been ill. The KJV names him Berodachbaladan in 2 Kings 20:12 and Merodachbaladan in Isaiah 39:1. Kings says Hezekiah hearkened to the visitors; Isaiah says he was glad of them. Isaiah also says Hezekiah had recovered. A Babylonian chronicle records Merodach-baladan's reign, but does not report this embassy.
record.text: KJV 2 Kings 20:12: “At that time Berodachbaladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present unto Hezekiah: for he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick.”
record.reasoning: The chronicle names Merodach-baladan, also called Marduk-apal-iddin, as king of Babylon. He is generally identified with the king in Kings and Isaiah. It records his accession, twelve-year reign and flight to Elam after Sargon fights him. It also reports later conflict under Sennacherib. These events support the reign setting, not an embassy date or motive. In 2 Chronicles 32:31, the visitors ask about a wonder in the land. That account says God left Hezekiah to test him.
record.scope: The compared biblical passages give no year for the embassy. This record does not choose between the king's first and later reign. It makes no claim about a KJV margin. The English names are the spellings in the packaged KJV. The Hebrew names differ in more than their first letter: Kings also includes a letter absent from Isaiah. The two Hebrew verbs also differ. No quoted Latin form is presented as exact Hebrew. The chronicle neither confirms nor contradicts the embassy, and does not establish its motive.

record.title: Nebuchadnezzar's campaign against Egypt (567 BCE)
record.summary: A damaged Babylonian text reports a campaign against Egypt in Nebuchadnezzar's thirty-seventh year. The usual date is 568/567 BCE. The Egyptian king's name is partly restored as Amasis. Ezekiel and Jeremiah predict Nebuchadnezzar's attack on Egypt. This is a proposed comparison with those passages. They are predictions, not reports of the campaign.
record.text: KJV Ezekiel 29:19: “Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I will give the land of Egypt unto Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall take her multitude, and take her spoil, and take her prey; and it shall be the wages for his army.”
record.reasoning: Ezekiel 29:17–20 dates its message to the twenty-seventh year. It presents Egypt as payment for the army's work against Tyre. Ezekiel 30:10–12 and Jeremiah 43:8–13 and 46:13 also predict an attack on Egypt. Rogers's translation describes troops and battle, with gaps in the text. His tentative fragments about defeat and destruction do not establish conquest. The later transcription also keeps gaps and partly restores the king's name. It supports the limited campaign notice.
record.scope: The broken text does not establish that Egypt was conquered, taken or made a province. It does not settle whether the predictions were fulfilled or failed. A missing or unclear result cannot decide that question. The newer author draws wider conclusions about history. This record does not adopt them. The existing Tyre record compares biblical passages internally. This History record concerns only the Egypt fragment and its proposed link with these texts. The date belongs to the reported campaign, not a date stated in the prophetic passages.

sources.label: Rogers (1912), Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'Nebuchadrezzar's Campaign against Egypt (567 B.C.)', text and translation of the British Museum fragment (Internet Archive scan, opened)
Aren M. Wilson-Wright, Jeremiah’s Egypt, pp. 31–32: fragmentary campaign text and restored name

record.title: The Refuge Residence Rule In Two Editions
record.summary: The KJV includes a rule about staying until the high priest dies. The old Greek translation lacks that rule here.
record.text:
packaged KJV, Joshua 20:4: “And when he that doth flee unto one of those cities shall stand at the entering of the gate of the city, and shall declare his cause in the ears of the elders of that city, they shall take him into the city unto them, and give him a place, that he may dwell among them.” Source: https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/JOS20.htm
packaged KJV, Joshua 20:5: “And if the avenger of blood pursue after him, then they shall not deliver the slayer up into his hand; because he smote his neighbour unwittingly, and hated him not beforetime.” Source: https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/JOS20.htm
packaged KJV, Joshua 20:6: “And he shall dwell in that city, until he stand before the congregation for judgment, and until the death of the high priest that shall be in those days: then shall the slayer return, and come unto his own city, and unto his own house, unto the city from whence he fled.” Source: https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/JOS20.htm
Brenton Greek edition, Joshua 20:3: “Φυγαδευτήριον τῷ φονευτῇ τῷ πατάξαντι ψυχὴν ἀκουσίως· καὶ ἔσονται ὑμῖν αἱ πόλεις φυγαδευτήριον, καὶ οὐκ ἀποθανεῖται ὁ φονευτὴς ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀγχιστεύοντος τὸ αἷμα, ἕως ἂν καταστῇ· ἐναντίον τῆς συναγωγῆς εἰς κρίσιν.” Source: https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS20.htm
Brenton Greek edition, Joshua 20:7: “Καὶ διέστειλε τὴν Κάδης ἐν τῇ Γαλιλαίᾳ ἐν τῷ ὄρει τῷ Νεφθαλὶ, καὶ Συχὲμ ἐν τῷ ὄρει τῷ Ἐφραὶμ, καὶ τὴν πόλιν Ἀρβὸκ, αὕτη ἐστὶ Χεβρὼν, ἐν τῷ ὄρει τῷ Ἰούδα.” Source: https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS20.htm
Brenton Greek edition, Joshua 20:9: “Αὗται αἱ πόλεις αἱ ἐπίκλητοι τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ καὶ τῷ προσηλύτῳ τῷ προσκειμένῳ ἐν αὐτοῖς, καταφυγεῖν ἐκεῖ παντὶ παίοντι ψυχὴν ἀκουσίως, ἵνα μὴ ἀποθάνῃ ἐν χειρὶ τοῦ ἀγχιστεύοντος τὸ αἷμα, ἕως ἄν καταστῇ ἔναντι τῆς συναγωγῆς εἰς κρίσιν.” Source: https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS20.htm
Brenton English translation, Joshua 20:3: “Even a refuge to the slayer who has smitten a man unintentionally; and the cities shall be to you a refuge, and the slayer shall not be put to death by the avenger of blood, until he have stood before the congregation for judgment.” Source: https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/JOS20.htm
Brenton English translation, Joshua 20:7: “And Joshua separated Cades in Galilee in the mount Nephthali, and Sychem in the mount Ephraim, and the city of Arboc; this is Chebron, in the mountain of Juda.” Source: https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/JOS20.htm
Brenton English translation, Joshua 20:9: “These were the cities selected for the sons of Israel, and for the stranger abiding among them, that every one who smites a soul unintentionally should flee thither, that he should not die by the hand of the avenger of blood, until he should stand before the congregation for judgment.” Source: https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/JOS20.htm
record.reasoning: The Greek page prints verses 1, 2, 3, 7, 8 and 9. It includes judgment before the community but omits the high priest’s death as the condition for returning home.
record.scope: This comparison concerns Joshua 20:6 in these editions. The Greek’s shorter chapter does not prove the rule was unknown elsewhere. Numbers 35:25-28 also gives the residence rule. The comparison does not establish which form is earlier or whether all ancient copies agree.

record.title: A Secret Message Or An Accusation About Truth
record.summary: The KJV describes a message secretly received. The old Greek translation first questions whether the listener’s words contained any truth.
record.text:
packaged KJV, Job 4:12: “Now a thing was secretly brought to me, and mine ear received a little thereof.” Source: https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/JOB04.htm
Brenton Greek edition, Job 4:12: “Εἰ δέ τι ῥῆμα ἀληθινὸν ἐγεγόνει ἐν λόγοις σου, οὐθὲν ἄν σοι τούτων κακὸν ἀπήντησε· πότερον οὐ δέξεταί μου τὸ οὖς ἐξαίσια παρʼ αὐτοῦ;” Source: https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB04.htm
Brenton English translation, Job 4:12: “But if there had been any truth in thy words, none of these evils would have befallen thee. Shall not mine ear receive excellent revelations from him?” Source: https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/JOB04.htm
record.reasoning: The Greek links the listener’s suffering to the truth of his words, adding a specific accusation.
record.scope: The comparison concerns Job 4:12 in these editions. It does not settle the Hebrew wording or identify the earliest form. A digital edition does not show that all ancient copies agree. This is poetic speech, not an independent account of physical events.
record.languageContext: Old Greek translation · Brenton Greek and English editions

record.title: New Testimony Or Renewed Torture
record.summary: The KJV describes renewed testimony against Job. The old Greek translation describes renewed torture.
record.text:

record.title: Mesha And Israel’s Rule
record.summary: Kings links Moab’s revolt with Ahab’s death. Mesha’s stone describes Moab regaining land held by Israel. Both concern conflict between these kingdoms. This comparison does not establish that they describe the same stage of that conflict.
record.reasoning: The Louvre identifies the stone as a record of Mesha’s victories. Its date fields differ within the ninth century BCE. The cited translation mentions Omri’s son and forty years. Those details need review before matching the accounts year by year.
record.scope: A royal victory record gives one ruler’s account. It does not independently confirm every event in Kings. This draft assigns no precise year. It does not identify the unnamed son or resolve the forty years.

record.title: Samaria In Kings And Sargon’s Account
record.summary: Kings reports Samaria’s capture by the king of Assyria. Sargon’s inscription also claims the city’s capture and removal of people. This gives an outside royal claim about Samaria. The relationship between these accounts still needs a chronology review.
record.reasoning: The current edition prints 27,290 people in one copy. Its notes record different totals in other copies. The account names Sargon as the speaker. Kings names Shalmaneser earlier in the campaign, then refers to the king of Assyria.
record.scope: A claim by Sargon does not settle who first captured the city. Differing copies limit the precision of the total. This draft does not force the two campaigns into one year. It does not turn royal claims into independently verified counts.

record.name: Jethro
record.summary: The priest of Midian whose daughter Zipporah marries Moses. Exodus says he gives Moses refuge and releases him to return to Egypt. He later brings Moses' wife and sons to the camp at the mountain of God. He praises the Lord after hearing of Israel's escape from Egypt and offers sacrifices. He advises Moses to appoint officials to share the work of judging the people. Exodus uses Jethro and Reuel; Numbers 10:29 uses Raguel. These name links do not settle Hobab's relationship to Moses.

children: Seven daughters in all (Exodus 2:16; only Zipporah is named)

residence: The camp at the mountain of God (Exodus 18:5)

record.name: Zipporah
record.summary: A daughter of the Midianite priest who becomes Moses' wife and bears Gershom and Eliezer. On the journey, she circumcises her son after the Lord threatens a man's life. Exodus 4:24 uses “him” without naming the man. She uses a sharp stone and speaks of a “bloody husband”. Exodus 18:2 says Moses had sent her back but does not say when. Her father brings her and her sons to Moses at the mountain of God.

residence: Her father's house after being sent back (Exodus 18:2)
The camp at the mountain of God (Exodus 18:5)

record.name: Eleazar
record.summary: Aaron's third-named son, who becomes high priest after his two older brothers and Aaron die. Numbers places Aaron's death on Mount Hor, where Moses puts Aaron's garments on Eleazar. He works with Moses during the census and the war against Midian. Later, he helps divide the land with Joshua.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; named among Aaron's sons in Exodus 6:23.

linked_stories.title: Aaron and His Sons Are Ordained
Edom Refuses Passage and Aaron Dies
A New Census and Joshua Appointed

record.name: Phinehas
record.summary: Eleazar's son. Numbers describes an Israelite bringing a Midianite woman into the camp during a plague at Shittim. Phinehas takes a javelin and kills them both. In the account, the Lord says he turned away wrath. The Lord promises him peace and a lasting priesthood. He later carries sacred objects during the war against Midian. He leads the group sent to the eastern tribes during the altar dispute.

record.name: Caleb
record.summary: Jephunneh's son, whom Numbers calls a Kenezite and a man of Judah. He is one of twelve men sent to spy out Canaan and urges Israel to go up at once. He and Joshua tear their clothes when the people refuse. Numbers says he survives the wilderness generation because he followed the Lord fully. At eighty-five, he asks for the hill country of Hebron and drives out the sons of Anak. This profile does not identify him with the Caleb in 1 Chronicles 2:18.

geography.origin: A Kenezite of the tribe of Judah (Numbers 13:6; Numbers 32:12)
residence: Sent from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land (Joshua 14:7)

linked_stories.title: Tribes Settle East of the Jordan

record.name: Korah
record.summary: A Levite from Kohath's family and a son of Izhar. In Numbers 16, he gathers followers with Dathan, Abiram and 250 leaders against Moses and Aaron. They say the whole community is holy. The account describes the earth swallowing Korah's company and fire consuming the 250 who offered incense. Numbers 26:11 says Korah's children did not die. These accounts are not combined into a more detailed death sequence here.

geography.origin: A Levite, son of Izhar, son of Kohath (Numbers 16:1)
residence: The wilderness camp, near the tabernacle (Numbers 16:19)

record.name: Balaam
record.summary: Beor's son from Pethor, whom Balak king of Moab calls to curse Israel. Numbers describes an angel and a speaking donkey before Balaam is allowed to go. From Moab's heights he blesses Israel instead, including a message about a star from Jacob. Numbers 31 links him to Israel's actions at Peor and says Israel killed him in the war against Midian. Second Peter and Revelation also criticize him.

geography.origin: Pethor, by the river of his people (Numbers 22:5)
residence: The heights of Moab overlooking Israel (Numbers 22:41)

record.name: Balak
record.summary: The son of Zippor and king of Moab, alarmed by Israel's defeat of the Amorites and its numbers. He sends for Balaam to curse Israel and takes him to a series of high places. Each message blesses Israel instead. Numbers 24:10 describes Balak's anger.

record.name: Nadab
record.summary: Aaron's firstborn son, who goes up the mountain with Moses and Aaron. Exodus says they see the God of Israel. Nadab is appointed a priest. Leviticus says he and Abihu offer fire the Lord had not commanded, and fire from the Lord consumes them. Numbers says they die without children.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; named among Aaron's sons in Exodus 6:23.

linked_stories.title: Aaron and His Sons Are Ordained

record.name: Abihu
record.summary: Aaron's second-named son, who goes up the mountain with Moses. Exodus says they see the God of Israel. He is appointed a priest. Leviticus says he and Nadab offer uncommanded fire in incense holders and die before the Lord.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; named among Aaron's sons in Exodus 6:23.

linked_stories.title: Aaron and His Sons Are Ordained

record.name: Hur
record.summary: A man who stands with Aaron during the battle with Amalek and helps hold up Moses' hands until sunset. When Moses goes up the mountain, he leaves Hur with Aaron to settle disputes. Exodus 31:2 names a Hur as Bezaleel's grandfather. It does not establish that this is the same Hur.

geography.origin: Birthplace and tribe not stated in the cited Exodus account.
residence: The camp, while Moses is on the mountain (Exodus 24:14)

linked_stories.title: Water from the Rock and the Battle with Amalek

record.name: Bezaleel
record.summary: A craftsman from Judah, son of Uri and grandson of Hur. Exodus says the Lord calls him by name and fills him with God's spirit, wisdom and skill. With Aholiab of Dan, he makes the sacred tent, its furnishings and the priests' garments as commanded.

geography.origin: Tribe of Judah, son of Uri, son of Hur (Exodus 31:2)

record.name: Rahab
record.summary: A woman of Jericho whom Joshua describes as a sex worker. She hides two spies on her roof, misleads the king's men and lowers the spies through her window. She says fear of Israel has fallen on the land and asks for kindness to her father's household. Joshua says she and her family survive Jericho's fall, and she lives among Israel. Matthew names Rachab in its family list; Hebrews and James also name Rahab. These later references do not establish every proposed family link here.

residence: A house on the town wall of Jericho (Joshua 2:15)

record.name: Achan
record.summary: A man of Judah who takes goods set apart at Jericho: a garment, silver and gold. He hides them in his tent, and Israel later loses at Ai. Joshua describes groups being selected until Achan is singled out. He admits wanting and taking the goods. The account describes stoning and burning in the valley of Achor. Its pronouns are not used here to settle exactly who or what is burned.

residence: Israel's camp at Jericho and Ai (Joshua 7:1)
Valley of Achor, where he is buried under stones (Joshua 7:26)

record.name: Othniel
record.summary: Kenaz's son, who captures a town and receives Caleb's daughter Achsah as his wife. The phrase “younger brother” can refer to Kenaz or Othniel; this profile does not choose between them. Judges says Israel cries out under Chushanrishathaim of Mesopotamia. The Lord raises Othniel as a deliverer, and the Lord's spirit comes on him. The account gives the land forty years of rest until his death.

geography.origin: Not stated beyond his family of Kenaz (Judges 3:9)

record.name: Ehud
record.summary: A left-handed man of Benjamin and son of Gera. Judges says the Lord raises him when Israel cries out under Eglon king of Moab. He brings tribute to Eglon, then returns to kill him with a dagger and escapes. He rallies Israel, which defeats Moab. Judges gives the land eighty years of rest. This profile does not identify him with the other Ehud in Chronicles.

record.name: Deborah
record.summary: A prophet and the wife of Lapidoth who judges Israel beneath a palm tree in Ephraim's hill country. She calls Barak to lead ten thousand men against Sisera and agrees to go with him. Judges records her warning that the Lord will give Sisera into a woman's hand. Judges 5:1 names Deborah and Barak as singers of the victory song. This Deborah is distinct from Rebekah's nurse.

geography.origin: Not stated; she held court in the hill country of Ephraim (Judges 4:5)
residence: Under the palm tree of Deborah, between Ramah and Bethel (Judges 4:5)

record.name: Barak
record.summary: Abinoam's son from Kedesh-naphtali, called by Deborah to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor against Sisera. He insists that she go with him. She warns that the honour of victory will pass to a woman. He pursues Sisera and finds him dead in Jael's tent. Hebrews 11:32 later names Barak among people it praises for faith.

residence: Mount Tabor, where he musters the army (Judges 4:6)

record.name: Jael
record.summary: The wife of Heber the Kenite. Judges says Sisera flees to her tent after his army's defeat, since Jabin and Heber's household are at peace. She welcomes him and drives a tent nail through his temples while he sleeps. She shows Barak the dead man. The song in Judges 5 blesses her above women in tents.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; she lives in Heber's tent in Judges 4:17.

record.name: Gideon
record.summary: Joash's son, an Abiezrite from Manasseh. Judges describes an angel calling him to save Israel while he threshes wheat in a winepress. He asks for a sign with a fleece. He reduces his army to three hundred and defeats Midian with trumpets and torches in jars. He refuses to rule but makes an ephod, an object used in worship whose precise form is not given. Judges calls it a trap for Israel and his household. The text lists seventy sons, then introduces Abimelech separately; no revised total is supplied here.

children: Abimelech, by a concubine at Shechem

record.name: Abimelech
record.summary: Gideon's son by a concubine from Shechem, a partner distinct from a wife. His mother's relatives support his claim to rule. Judges 9:5 says he kills seventy brothers on one stone, while also saying Jotham survives. The people make him king at Shechem. Judges says God sends an evil spirit between him and Shechem's men. He destroys the city. At Thebez, a woman breaks his skull with a millstone. The text calls his death God's repayment for his wickedness.

siblings: Seventy brothers in Judges 9:5, which also says Jotham survived

record.name: Jephthah
record.summary: A warrior from Gilead, whose parents are Gilead and a woman the text calls a harlot. The elders call him back to lead against Ammon. Judges says the Lord's spirit comes on him. He vows, or promises, to offer whoever first leaves his house to greet him as a burnt offering. His only daughter comes out first. The text says he acts according to his vow; this profile does not settle sacrifice versus dedication. He later fights Ephraim at the Jordan crossings and judges Israel for six years.

record.name: Samson
record.summary: Manoah's son from Dan, announced as set apart for God from birth. Judges says he will begin to free Israel from the Philistines. He marries a Philistine woman from Timnath, kills many Philistines and judges Israel for twenty years. Samson tells Delilah that shaving his hair will take away his strength. Judges 16:20 also says the Lord has left him. He is shaved, blinded and made to grind in Gaza's prison. At the Philistine temple, he asks to die with them and brings the building down.

geography.origin: Zorah, of the family of the Danites (Judges 13:2)

record.name: Delilah
record.summary: A woman Samson loves in the valley of Sorek. Judges 16 says the Philistine rulers ask her to draw out the source of his strength. She presses him until he tells her. She lets him sleep on her knees and calls a man to shave his seven locks. The account says his strength then leaves him. It does not give her birthplace or ethnic identity.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; the account places her in the valley of Sorek (Judges 16:4).

record.name: Naomi
record.summary: Elimelech's wife from Bethlehem, who moves to Moab during a famine. There she loses her husband and her sons Mahlon and Chilion. She returns to Bethlehem with her daughter-in-law Ruth. She asks to be called Mara, saying the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her. She guides Ruth toward Boaz. When Obed is born, the neighbours say a son is born to Naomi. Their words in Ruth 4:17 do not make Naomi his birth mother.

linked_stories.title: Naomi and Ruth Return to Bethlehem

record.name: Ruth
record.summary: A Moabite woman who marries Mahlon, Naomi's son. After his death, she stays with Naomi and says Naomi's people and God will be hers. In Bethlehem, she gathers grain left by harvesters in the field of Boaz, a relative. Following Naomi's advice, she asks him to act as a close relative at the threshing floor. The account describes the nearer relative declining the family and land arrangement. Boaz marries her, and she bears Obed, Jesse's father and David's grandfather. Matthew names her in its family list.

linked_stories.title: Naomi and Ruth Return to Bethlehem

record.name: Boaz
record.summary: A wealthy relative of Elimelech in Bethlehem who lets Ruth gather grain left in his field. At the threshing floor, she asks him to spread his skirt over her as a close relative. He arranges to buy the family land at the town gate. He marries Ruth to preserve the dead man's name through his inheritance. Their son Obed is Jesse's father. Matthew names Booz as the son of Salmon and Rachab. That family list does not itself settle further claims about Rachab's identity.

record.name: Hannah
record.summary: One of Elkanah's two wives from Ramathaim-zophim. She has no children, and Peninnah taunts her. At Shiloh, Eli first mistakes her intense prayer for drunkenness. She promises to give a son to the Lord. She bears Samuel and brings him to Shiloh after he stops nursing, leaving him there to serve. First Samuel 2 opens with her prayer of praise. The account later gives her three more sons and two daughters.

children: Three more sons and two daughters (unnamed; 1 Samuel 2:21)

linked_stories.title: Hannah and the Birth of Samuel

record.name: Eli
record.summary: The priest at Shiloh who watches Hannah pray and later trains the child Samuel. First Samuel calls his sons Hophni and Phinehas “sons of Belial”, a harsh description of their wrongdoing. They misuse their office. Eli rebukes them but does not stop them. An unnamed man of God warns of judgment on Eli's family. The account later describes the Lord giving Samuel a similar warning. At ninety-eight, Eli hears that the ark is taken and his sons are dead. He falls from his seat and dies. The text says he judged Israel forty years.

geography.origin: Shiloh, where he sits at the temple of the Lord (1 Samuel 1:9)

linked_stories.title: Hannah and the Birth of Samuel

record.name: Samuel
record.summary: Elkanah and Hannah's son, given to serve the Lord at Shiloh under Eli. First Samuel describes the Lord calling him as a child. The text presents him as a prophet known from Dan to Beersheba. He judges Israel on a yearly circuit and lives at Ramah. He anoints Saul as leader and later anoints David among his brothers. He rebukes Saul, saying obedience is better than sacrifice. The book covers the end of the judges and the start of the kingdom. It says Samuel judged Israel throughout his life.

linked_stories.title: Hannah and the Birth of Samuel

record.name: Saul
record.summary: Kish's son from Benjamin, described as taller than any other man in Israel. Samuel anoints him, and he becomes Israel's first king. He fights the Philistines. Samuel says the Lord has rejected him as king for failing to keep the Lord's word. David enters his service. First Samuel 18:8–12 describes Saul's anger and fear; the later account follows his pursuit of David. When the Lord no longer answers, he consults a medium at Endor. Archers wound him on Mount Gilboa, and he falls on his sword. Jonathan and two other sons die that day.

residence: Mount Gilboa, where he dies (1 Samuel 31:1)

linked_stories.title: Saul and the Medium at Endor; Saul's Death

record.name: Jonathan
record.summary: Saul's son and David's friend. He and his armour carrier attack a Philistine outpost without telling Saul. The people later refuse to let Saul put Jonathan to death. He and David make a lasting agreement. Jonathan gives David his robe, sword and bow and warns him of Saul's plans. He says David will be king, with himself next in rank. He dies with Saul at Gilboa. David's song of grief calls Jonathan's love wonderful.

residence: Gibeah, in his father's house (1 Samuel 14:2)
Mount Gilboa, where he dies (1 Samuel 31:2)

linked_stories.title: Saul and the Medium at Endor; Saul's Death

record.name: David
record.summary: Jesse's youngest son from Bethlehem, summoned from the sheep and then anointed by Samuel. He kills Goliath with a sling and stone and serves Saul. He later flees Saul, leading an outlaw group in the wilderness and at Ziklag. After Saul's death, he becomes king at Hebron. The account gives him seven and a half years there and thirty-three in Jerusalem. It describes the Lord promising him a lasting royal line and throne. Nathan confronts him over Bathsheba and Uriah's death. The book also describes Absalom's revolt. The New Testament names David in Jesus' family list and Paul's speech at Antioch.

geography.origin: Bethlehem of Judah, son of Jesse (1 Samuel 17:12)
residence: The cave Adullam and the wilderness (1 Samuel 22:1)
Jerusalem, the city of David (2 Samuel 5:7)

linked_stories.title: Saul and the Medium at Endor; Saul's Death

record.name: Michal
record.summary: Saul's younger daughter, who loves David. Saul gives her to David after he brings back two hundred Philistine foreskins. When Saul sends men to kill David, she lowers David through a window. He escapes. Saul later gives her to Phalti son of Laish. David demands her return through Abner and Ishbosheth. When the ark enters Jerusalem, she sees David dancing and despises him in her heart. Second Samuel 6:23 says she had no child until her death. This profile does not settle that statement against 2 Samuel 21:8.

residence: The house of David in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:16)

record.name: Abigail
record.summary: Nabal's wife from Carmel, whom First Samuel describes as having good understanding. Nabal is described as harsh. After he insults David's men, Abigail brings David bread, wine, sheep, grain, raisins and figs without telling Nabal. About ten days later, Nabal dies. David then sends for Abigail, and she becomes his wife. Second Samuel 3:3 names their son Chileab; the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 3:1 names him Daniel.

geography.origin: Carmel, the home of Nabal (1 Samuel 25:3)

record.name: Bathsheba
record.summary: Eliam's daughter and Uriah the Hittite's wife in Second Samuel. First Chronicles' parallel family list uses the names Bathshua and Ammiel; the name link is not proved here. David sees Bathsheba from his roof, sends for her and has sex with her. She conceives; David arranges Uriah's death and marries her. Their first child dies. She later bears Solomon, whom the text says the Lord loved. With Nathan, she raises the succession with the ageing David, who promises Solomon the throne. Solomon later seats her at his right hand. Matthew calls her the wife of Urias.

geography.origin: Not stated; daughter of Eliam (2 Samuel 11:3)

record.name: Nathan
record.summary: A prophet at David's court, distinct from David's son of that name. In Second Samuel 7, he first supports David's plan for a house for the ark. He changes his answer after receiving the Lord's word. He tells David about a rich man taking a poor man's lamb, then says, “Thou art the man”. David confesses, and Nathan says the Lord has put away his sin. The name Jedidiah is given to the child through Nathan. Later, Nathan joins Bathsheba in urging David to make Solomon king. David directs Nathan and Zadok to anoint Solomon.

record.name: Absalom
record.summary: David's third son, born at Hebron to Maacah, the daughter of Geshur's king. Second Samuel praises his beauty. He has Amnon killed after Amnon rapes his sister Tamar, then flees to Geshur for three years. Joab brings him back. He wins over people seeking the king's judgment and proclaims himself king at Hebron. David leaves Jerusalem. Absalom catches his head in an oak and is killed by Joab and ten armour carriers. David mourns him with “O my son Absalom”. The account names three sons and a daughter; this profile does not settle that against 2 Samuel 18:18.

children: Three sons (unnamed) and a daughter, Tamar

residence: Geshur, with his mother's father (2 Samuel 13:38)
Hebron, where he is proclaimed king (2 Samuel 15:10)

record.name: Joab
record.summary: Zeruiah's son, brother of Abishai and Asahel, and commander of David's army. Second Samuel says he kills Abner to avenge Asahel. He later kills Amasa and strikes Absalom with darts against David's wishes. David calls Zeruiah's sons too hard for him. Joab supports Adonijah in the struggle for the throne; he had not supported Absalom. Following David's charge, Solomon orders Benaiah to kill Joab beside the altar. Joab is buried at his own house in the wilderness.

geography.origin: Not stated; his brother Asahel is buried at Bethlehem (2 Samuel 2:32)
residence: Camp and campaign for David (2 Samuel 8:16)
The tabernacle of the Lord, where he catches the altar's horns (1 Kings 2:28)

record.name: Solomon
record.summary: David and Bathsheba's son, also given the name Jedidiah because of the Lord. He becomes king after David, despite Adonijah's attempt to take the throne. He asks God for understanding to judge the people. The account says God gives him wisdom and further gifts he did not request. He builds the temple over seven years. Kings lists seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, partners distinct from wives. It says his heart turns toward other gods in old age. It gives him forty years as king in Jerusalem.

geography.origin: Jerusalem, born to David and Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12:24)

linked_stories.title: The Queen of Sheba and Solomon's Decline

record.name: Mephibosheth
record.summary: Jonathan's son, whose feet are disabled after his nurse drops him while fleeing when he is five. David restores Saul's land to him and gives him a place at the king's table for Jonathan's sake. During Absalom's revolt, Ziba says Mephibosheth stayed behind hoping to gain the kingdom. David gives Ziba his goods. On David's return, Mephibosheth says Ziba deceived him. David tells them to divide the land; Mephibosheth says Ziba can take it all. This profile does not decide between their accounts. A parallel family list uses Meribbaal; he is distinct from the Mephibosheth in 2 Samuel 21:8.

residence: Lo-debar, before David summoned him (2 Samuel 9:4)
Jerusalem, eating at the king's table (2 Samuel 9:13)

record.name: Uriah
record.summary: Bathsheba's husband, called a Hittite and listed among David's thirty-seven leading warriors. David orders Joab to place him where the battle is fiercest and withdraw so he will be killed. Uriah dies during the siege. Joab's message anticipates David's anger. Matthew refers to him as Urias. The Hittite label does not establish his birthplace.

geography.origin: Not stated; called a Hittite (2 Samuel 11:3)
residence: Jerusalem, near the king's house (2 Samuel 11:3)
The siege of Rabbah, where he dies (2 Samuel 11:17)

record.name: Rehoboam
record.summary: Solomon's son by Naamah the Ammonite, who becomes king at Shechem at forty-one. The people ask him to ease the burdens Solomon imposed. He rejects the elders' advice for that of his young peers. He promises “scorpions” where Solomon used whips. Ten tribes leave him, while Judah and Benjamin remain. Kings says a message through Shemaiah stops him from attacking Israel. In his fifth year, Shishak of Egypt takes treasures from the temple and royal house. War with Jeroboam continues throughout his reign.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; rules from Jerusalem (1 Kings 14:21).

linked_stories.title: The Man of God from Judah

record.name: Jeroboam
record.summary: Nebat and Zeruah's son from Zereda, called an Ephrathite. Solomon puts him over the labour force of Joseph's tribes. Ahijah tears a garment into twelve pieces and gives him ten, with a conditional promise of a lasting royal line. Solomon seeks to kill him, so he flees to Egypt until Solomon dies. The people call him back and make him king at Shechem. He sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, appoints priests outside Levi and establishes an eighth-month feast. Kings uses his sin to judge later rulers. He reigns twenty-two years, followed by his son Nadab.

residence: Shechem, which he built in mount Ephraim (1 Kings 12:25)
Egypt, in flight from Solomon (1 Kings 11:40)

linked_stories.title: The Man of God from Judah

record.name: Ahab
record.summary: Omri's son, who rules Israel from Samaria for twenty-two years. Kings says he does more evil than all before him. He marries Jezebel, Ethbaal's daughter, and serves Baal. Elijah announces a drought, meets him on Carmel and confronts him after Naboth's death. Ahab then humbles himself. While fighting Syria at Ramoth-gilead, an arrow shot at random strikes him. Kings says he dies that evening in his chariot and dogs lick the blood washed from it. This profile does not settle Athaliah's parentage or identify Ahab with Jeremiah's Ahab.

children: Daughter, wife of Jehoram of Judah (2 Kings 8:18)

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; rules from Samaria (1 Kings 16:29).
residence: Jezreel, where Naboth's vineyard lay (1 Kings 21:1)

record.name: Jezebel
record.summary: Ethbaal's daughter and Ahab's wife. Kings says Ahab marries Jezebel and serves Baal. It describes her killing the Lord's prophets and supporting four hundred prophets of the groves. She threatens Elijah's life after Carmel. Using letters sealed with Ahab's seal, she arranges false charges against Naboth and his death by stoning. When Jehu reaches Jezreel, she paints her face and looks from a window. Court servants throw her down, and she is trampled. Only her skull, feet and palms remain when people come to bury her. Jehu links this to Elijah's words about dogs eating her flesh.

record.name: Jehu
record.summary: Son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi, serving as a commander at Ramoth-gilead. A prophet sent by Elisha anoints him king of Israel. He shoots Joram at Naboth's plot, orders Ahaziah struck down and sees Jezebel thrown from her window. He has Ahab's seventy sons killed at Samaria and destroys Baal's worshippers and temple. Kings describes the Lord promising his descendants four generations on the throne. It also criticizes his continued calf worship and incomplete obedience. He reigns twenty-eight years. His father's name does not identify him with King Jehoshaphat of Judah.

geography.origin: Ramoth-gilead, as captain among the host (2 Kings 9:1)

record.name: Athaliah
record.summary: Ahaziah of Judah's mother. Second Kings 8:26 calls her Omri's daughter; 8:18 calls Jehoram's wife Ahab's daughter. These labels do not settle the exact family relationship here. After Ahaziah dies, she attacks the royal family. Jehosheba, Joram's daughter and Ahaziah's sister, hides the infant Joash in the temple for six years while Athaliah rules. In the seventh year, Jehoiada makes an agreement with the captains and guards and crowns Joash. Athaliah is taken out and killed near the horses' entrance to the royal house.

geography.origin: Israel, daughter of the house of Omri (2 Kings 8:26)

record.name: Naaman
record.summary: A Syrian commander whom Second Kings describes as honoured and brave, but affected by leprosy. A captive Israelite girl tells his wife about the prophet in Samaria. Naaman travels with his king's letter. Elisha tells him to wash seven times in the Jordan. He is angry, but follows his servants' advice and washes. The account says he is healed. He declares that God is found only in Israel and takes earth home for worship. He asks pardon for bowing in Rimmon's temple while attending his master. Jesus mentions Naaman while discussing lepers in Israel during Elisha's time.

geography.origin: Syria, captain of the host of its king (2 Kings 5:1)
residence: The Jordan, where he washes (2 Kings 5:14)

record.name: Hezekiah
record.summary: Ahaz and Abi's son, who becomes Judah's king at twenty-five and reigns twenty-nine years. He removes shrines and images and breaks Moses' bronze serpent, which people had used for worship. He calls it Nehushtan. When Sennacherib attacks Judah's towns, Hezekiah pays the demand. He later prays after an Assyrian official's challenge. Kings describes the Lord's angel striking the Assyrian camp. In the illness account, Isaiah tells him to prepare for death. He prays and receives fifteen more years, with a backward-moving shadow as a sign. After he shows Babylonian envoys his treasures, Isaiah warns they will be carried to Babylon. These episodes do not establish an independent chronology here.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; rules from Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:2).

linked_stories.title: Hezekiah's Illness and the Babylonian Envoys

record.name: Manasseh
record.summary: Hezekiah's son, who becomes Judah's king at twelve and reigns fifty-five years. Kings describes him restoring shrines, building altars for Baal and heavenly bodies, and making his son pass through fire. It also describes his dealings with spirits and the innocent blood he sheds in Jerusalem. Kings reports a warning of disaster for Jerusalem because of his sins. Chronicles adds an account of Assyrian captains taking him in chains to Babylon. It says he humbles himself there and returns to Jerusalem. His son Amon follows him.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; rules from Jerusalem (2 Kings 21:1).

record.name: Josiah
record.summary: Amon and Jedidah's son, who becomes Judah's king at eight and reigns thirty-one years. Kings says he does right in the Lord's sight. In his eighteenth year, Hilkiah finds the law book in the temple. Josiah tears his clothes and sends to Huldah, a prophet. He reads the book to the people and makes an agreement to follow it. He removes idols and shrines in Judah and at Bethel. Kings links his actions at Bethel to an earlier prophet's words. It describes his Passover and his turning to the Lord as unequalled. Pharaoh-nechoh kills him at Megiddo.

linked_stories.title: The Man of God from Judah

record.name: Abner
record.summary: Ner's son and commander of Saul's army. First Samuel 14:50–51 supplies the family wording; this profile does not call Abner Saul's uncle. After Saul dies, Abner makes Ish-bosheth king at Mahanaim and leads his forces against David's men. During the fighting at Gibeon, he twice warns Asahel to stop pursuing him, then kills him with his spear. He quarrels with Ish-bosheth over Rizpah and offers to bring Israel over to David. David receives him at Hebron. Joab kills him at the gate; the account gives revenge for Asahel as the reason. David mourns publicly and walks behind his body.

record.name: Adonijah
record.summary: David's fourth son, born to Haggith after Absalom. As David ages, Adonijah declares he will be king, with chariots and fifty runners. Joab and Abiathar support him, and he holds a feast at En-rogel. Nathan and Bathsheba urge David to name Solomon. Adonijah flees to the altar and is spared on condition of good conduct. After David's death, he asks Bathsheba to request Abishag as his wife. Solomon sends Benaiah to kill him. This profile adds no hidden motive for Adonijah's request.

record.name: Amnon
record.summary: David's firstborn son, born at Hebron to Ahinoam. Second Samuel describes his desire for his half-sister Tamar and his distress. Following Jonadab's advice, he pretends to be ill and asks Tamar to bring food. He rapes her, then the account says his hatred exceeds his earlier desire. He has her thrown out. David is very angry, but this episode reports no action by him. Two years later, Absalom orders his servants to kill Amnon during a sheep-shearing feast while Amnon is drinking wine.

residence: Baal-hazor, where he is killed (2 Samuel 13:23)

record.name: Tamar, daughter of David
record.summary: David's daughter and Absalom's sister, whom Second Samuel describes as beautiful. She wears the special garment of the king's unmarried daughters. David sends her to prepare food for Amnon. She begs Amnon not to force her and says he could ask the king for her. Amnon rapes her and throws her out. She tears her garment, puts ashes on her head and cries aloud. Absalom takes her in, and the account describes her remaining desolate in his house. She is distinct from Judah's daughter-in-law and from Absalom's daughter Tamar in 2 Samuel 14:27.

geography.origin: Jerusalem, in the king's house (2 Samuel 13:7)

record.name: Cyrus
record.summary: King of Persia, whose first-year proclamation in Ezra permits Judeans to return and rebuild Jerusalem's temple. He says the God of heaven gave him his kingdoms and calls God's people to go. He asks neighbours to help with silver, gold and goods. He returns temple vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar, counting them out to Sheshbazzar. Ezra links this to Jeremiah's words. Isaiah calls Cyrus the Lord's anointed, and Daniel says Daniel prospers into his reign. These texts do not say every Judean returned or establish Cyrus's birthplace.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; king of Persia in Ezra 1:1.

linked_stories.title: The Fall of Judah and Cyrus's Decree

record.name: Zerubbabel
record.summary: A leader among those returning from Babylon. Ezra and Haggai call him Shealtiel's son, while 1 Chronicles 3:19 lists him among Pedaiah's sons. This profile leaves that difference unresolved and does not identify him with Sheshbazzar. With Jeshua, he builds the altar and lays the temple foundation in the second year. After work stops, messages from Haggai and Zechariah prompt them to begin again. Haggai calls him Judah's governor and describes the Lord promising to make him a signet, a seal of authority. Zechariah says he will finish the temple. Matthew places him in Jechonias's family line.

geography.origin: Babylon, among the returnees led out in Cyrus's time (Ezra 2:2)

record.name: Ezra
record.summary: A priest from Aaron's line through Seraiah and a trained reader and teacher of Moses' law. In Artaxerxes' seventh year, he leaves Babylon with the king's letter on the first day of the first month. Ezra 7:9 places his arrival in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month. The book says he prepares to study, follow and teach the law. After hearing about marriages to foreign women, he prays and weeps. Ezra 10:3 describes an agreement to send the women away. Nehemiah describes him reading the law to the people on the first day of the seventh month.

geography.origin: Priestly line of Aaron through Seraiah (Ezra 7:1-5)

record.name: Nehemiah
record.summary: Hachaliah's son, serving at Shushan when Hanani and others report Jerusalem's broken wall and the people's distress. He weeps, fasts and prays. In Artaxerxes' twentieth year, he serves the king's drink and asks to rebuild the city. He receives letters and timber. Nehemiah describes the wall builders facing opposition, carrying weapons as they work. He governs Judah for twelve years without taking the governor's food allowance. He later returns to the king, then comes back to make further reforms. This profile does not identify every Nehemiah in the records as this governor.

geography.origin: Shushan the palace, son of Hachaliah (Nehemiah 1:1)

record.name: Sanballat
record.summary: Called the Horonite in Nehemiah. With Tobiah and Geshem, he mocks the people rebuilding Jerusalem's wall. He speaks before Samaria's army. When the wall lacks only its doors, he sends four requests for Nehemiah to meet him near Ono. Nehemiah says they intend harm; this is Nehemiah's account of their purpose. Later, a son of Joiada from the high priest's family becomes Sanballat's son-in-law. Nehemiah drives that man away. The Horonite label is not used here to assign a modern nationality.

children: Daughter (unnamed), married into the high priest's family

residence: Samaria is named in his speech (Nehemiah 4:2)

record.name: Vashti
record.summary: Ahasuerus's queen, who holds a feast for women while he feasts with the princes. On the seventh day, the king is merry with wine. He sends seven court servants to bring her wearing the royal crown and display her beauty. She refuses, and he becomes angry. Esther gives no reason for her refusal. Memucan advises barring her from the king's presence and giving her position to another woman. A decree goes to every province. The later search for a queen leads to Esther taking her place.

geography.origin: Not stated in the text; queen of Ahasuerus (Esther 1:9)

record.name: Ahasuerus
record.summary: Esther's king ruling 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia, with his throne at Shushan. In his third year, he displays his riches for 180 days, then gives a seven-day feast. He removes Vashti and makes Esther queen in his seventh year. He promotes Haman and gives his ring for the decree against the Jews. After Esther reveals the plot, he orders Haman's death and gives the ring to Mordecai. The book later says he imposes tribute on the land and islands. This profile does not settle his external historical identity.

geography.origin: King of Persia, 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia (Esther 1:1)

record.name: Esther
record.summary: Hadassah, Abihail's daughter, whose cousin Mordecai raises her as his own daughter after her parents die. Esther says she enters the king's house in the tenth month of his seventh year and becomes queen. At Mordecai's direction, she keeps her people secret. When Haman's decree comes, Mordecai says help may come elsewhere and her position may be for this moment. She asks the Jews to fast three days and approaches the king without being called. The book describes two banquets, her naming Haman and a second decree for the Jews.

geography.origin: Jewish orphan in Shushan, daughter of Abihail (Esther 2:7, 2:15)

record.name: Mordecai
record.summary: Jair's son from Benjamin, living in Shushan and raising his cousin Esther. Esther traces his family through Shimei and Kish. He tells Esther to conceal her people, uncovers Bigthan and Teresh's plot and refuses to bow to Haman. When Haman's decree comes, he tears his clothes, wears mourning cloth and urges Esther to act. The king honours him publicly using Haman's own proposal. He later receives the king's ring. Esther puts him in charge of Haman's house, which the king gave to her.
