He writes about keeping Purim and becomes second to the king. This profile distinguishes him from Ezra's returnee Mordecai.

record.name: Haman
record.summary: Hammedatha's son, called an Agagite, whom Ahasuerus promotes above the princes. When Mordecai refuses to bow, Haman seeks to destroy Mordecai's people. He casts a lot to choose the day and offers the king ten thousand talents of silver. Despite his invitations to Esther's banquets, seeing Mordecai angers him. On advice from Zeresh and friends, he builds a gallows fifty cubits high. The king makes him lead Mordecai through the city in honour. Esther names him as the enemy, and he is hanged on his own gallows. His house goes to Esther, and his ten sons are killed.

record.name: Daniel
record.summary: A child of Judah taken to Babylon and renamed Belteshazzar. Daniel says he refuses the king's food and wine and receives understanding of dreams and visions from God. He explains Nebuchadnezzar's dream and is made ruler over Babylon's province. He reads the writing for Belshazzar. Under Darius, he is thrown into a lions' den for praying despite a decree. Later chapters describe beasts, a ram and goat, seventy weeks and a final vision in Cyrus's third year. Ezekiel names a Daniel with Noah and Job; the shared name does not settle his identity here. Matthew records Jesus referring to Daniel as a prophet.

linked_stories.title: Daniel and His Friends in Babylon

record.name: Nebuchadnezzar
record.summary: King of Babylon. Kings and Jeremiah describe his siege of Jerusalem, Jeconiah's captivity and the removal of temple vessels. His officers later burn the temple. Daniel describes his troubling dream of a statue and his promotion of Daniel over the wise men. He makes a gold image and orders three Judean men thrown into a furnace, then praises their God. Daniel also describes him living apart from people and eating grass like oxen. He later raises his eyes to heaven and praises its King. Cyrus returns the temple vessels he had taken. Daniel's father language about Belshazzar does not establish a biological link here.

linked_stories.title: Daniel and His Friends in Babylon
The Fall of Jerusalem and Flight to Egypt

record.name: Belshazzar
record.summary: Daniel calls him king of the Chaldeans. He feasts with a thousand lords and orders vessels taken from Jerusalem's temple brought out. The book describes a hand writing on the wall and his wise men failing to read it. The queen recalls Daniel. Daniel rebukes Belshazzar for not humbling himself despite knowing what happened to Nebuchadnezzar. Daniel reads and explains “Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin”. Belshazzar clothes him in scarlet but is killed that night. The book places other visions in Belshazzar's first and third years. Its father language for Nebuchadnezzar does not settle biological parentage here.

geography.origin: King of the Chaldeans; Nebuchadnezzar is called his father (Daniel 5:2, 5:22)

record.name: Jonah
record.summary: Amittai's son from Gathhepher, named as a prophet during Jeroboam son of Joash's reign. Jonah says the Lord sends him to Nineveh, but he flees toward Tarshish. Sailors throw him overboard during a storm. The book describes three days and nights in a great fish, where he prays. Sent again, he announces Nineveh's fall in forty days. The people believe God and fast. Jonah becomes angry and sits outside the city; the Lord asks whether Nineveh should be spared. The Gospels later describe Jesus speaking of Jonah's sign. This profile does not identify a fish species or make a science claim.

record.name: Isaiah
record.summary: Amoz's son, whose visions concern Judah and Jerusalem from Uzziah's reign to Hezekiah's. Isaiah describes seeing the Lord on a throne in the year Uzziah dies. He answers, “Here am I; send me”. He meets Ahaz with his son Shearjashub and offers the sign of Immanuel. Isaiah 8:3 describes a prophetess bearing his son without explicitly calling her his wife. Isaiah 20:3 describes his three years naked and barefoot as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia. He speaks to Hezekiah during the Assyrian crisis and his illness. He warns that Babylon will carry away Hezekiah's treasures and sons.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; his visions concern Judah and Jerusalem (Isaiah 1:1).

linked_stories.title: Ahaz and the Sign of Immanuel

record.name: Ahaz
record.summary: Jotham's son, who becomes Judah's king at twenty and reigns sixteen years in Jerusalem. Kings criticizes him for following Israel's kings, making his son pass through fire and offering sacrifices at shrines. When Syria and Israel threaten Jerusalem, Isaiah brings him a message to stay calm and not fear. Ahaz refuses the offered sign. Isaiah then gives the sign of Immanuel to David's family. This profile does not settle later readings of that sign. Hezekiah succeeds Ahaz.

linked_stories.title: Ahaz and the Sign of Immanuel

record.name: Sennacherib
record.summary: King of Assyria, whom the biblical account places attacking Judah's fortified towns in Hezekiah's fourteenth year. Hezekiah offers tribute. Sennacherib sends Rabshakeh and other officials with a large army to Jerusalem's upper pool. Isaiah describes the Lord's angel striking the Assyrian camp, leaving 185,000 dead. The account says Sennacherib returns to Nineveh. Later, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer kill him in his god's temple, and Esarhaddon succeeds him.

geography.origin: Assyria; his capital in the text is Nineveh (Isaiah 37:37)

record.name: Jeremiah
record.summary: Hilkiah's son from the priests at Anathoth in Benjamin. His book describes receiving the Lord's words from Josiah's thirteenth year until Jerusalem's captivity. Told he was appointed a prophet before birth, he objects that he is young and cannot speak. Pashur strikes him and puts him in stocks. He opposes Hananiah's message and has Baruch write down his words. During Jerusalem's last siege, he is lowered into a pit and rescued by Ebed-melech. He later joins the group taken into Egypt against his warning.

geography.origin: Anathoth in the land of Benjamin (Jeremiah 1:1)

linked_stories.title: The Fall of Jerusalem and Flight to Egypt

record.name: Baruch
record.summary: Neriah's son, who writes down Jeremiah's words. In Jehoiakim's fourth year, he records Jeremiah's spoken messages from the Lord on a scroll. After the king burns it, Baruch writes another at Jeremiah's direction, with further words added. The book says the Lord hides both men from arrest. A separate message to Baruch records his grief and lack of rest. After Jerusalem falls, he is taken into Egypt with Jeremiah. Shared family names do not expressly establish Seraiah as his brother.

linked_stories.title: The Fall of Jerusalem and Flight to Egypt

record.name: Hananiah son of Azur
record.summary: Azur's son, a prophet from Gibeon, distinct from Daniel's companion. In Zedekiah's fourth year, he speaks before priests and people in the temple. He announces that the Lord has broken Babylon's power. He predicts the return of temple vessels, Jeconiah and the captives within two years. Jeremiah replies that the Lord did not send him and that his message makes people trust a lie. Jeremiah 28 says Hananiah dies that year, in the seventh month.

record.name: Zedekiah
record.summary: Josiah and Hamutal's son, named Mattaniah before the king of Babylon renames him Zedekiah in 2 Kings 24:17. He becomes Judah's king at twenty-one and reigns eleven years. The account criticizes his rule and describes his revolt against Babylon. During the siege, he secretly asks Jeremiah for the Lord's word. He lets the princes put Jeremiah in a pit, then allows Ebed-melech to lift him out. He asks Jeremiah to keep their talks secret. Babylonian forces catch him near Jericho, kill his sons before him, blind him and take him to Babylon. Jeremiah says he remains imprisoned until death.

parents: Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah

linked_stories.title: The Fall of Jerusalem and Flight to Egypt

record.name: Ebed-melech
record.summary: A court servant whom Jeremiah calls an Ethiopian eunuch, using an ancient designation associated with Cush. This label does not assign him a modern nationality. He hears Jeremiah has been put in a pit and appeals to the king at Benjamin's gate. With permission, he takes thirty men and lowers cloth and ropes to lift Jeremiah out. Jeremiah remains in the prison court. Jeremiah 39:18 presents the Lord's promise to save Ebed-melech when the city falls. The stated reason is his trust in the Lord.

geography.origin: Called Ethiopian in Jeremiah 38:7, an ancient designation associated with Cush; no modern nationality is assigned.

record.name: Ezekiel
record.summary: Buzi's son and a priest among captives by the river Chebar in Chaldea. His book places its opening visions in the fifth year of Jehoiachin's captivity. It describes the heavens opening and visions of God. Addressed as “son of man”, Ezekiel is sent to speak and sits stunned among the exiles at Telabib. He is told to lie on his side as a sign of Israel's wrongdoing. The book describes his wife's death and a command not to mourn. Later, he describes the Spirit setting him in a valley of bones.

geography.origin: Priestly family, son of Buzi; among the exiles in Chaldea (Ezekiel 1:3)
residence: His house, with the elders of Judah (Ezekiel 8:1)

record.name: Hosea
record.summary: Beeri's son, whose book names four kings of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel. Hosea describes a command to marry a sexually unfaithful woman, followed by his marriage to Gomer. The children are named Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi, with each name carrying a message to Israel. Chapter 3 tells him to love a woman involved with another man. He buys her for silver and barley and tells her to wait for him. The book links these actions to the Lord's love for Israel. Chapter 3 does not name the woman as Gomer.

record.name: Gomer
record.summary: Diblaim's daughter, whom Hosea marries following the Lord's command in Hosea 1. She bears a son, then a daughter named Lo-ruhamah. After weaning her, she bears another son, Lo-ammi. Chapter 3 describes an unnamed woman involved with another man. Hosea buys her and tells her to remain with him. The passage does not state that she is Gomer.

record.name: Amos
record.summary: A herdsman from Tekoa whose words concern Israel during Uzziah's and Jeroboam son of Joash's reigns. Amos 1 places them two years before an earthquake. Amaziah, Bethel's priest, reports him to the king and tells him to stop speaking there and return to Judah. In Amos 7:14–15, Amos says he was neither a prophet nor a prophet's son. He describes tending herds and gathering sycomore fruit. He says the Lord took him from his flock and sent him to Israel. This prophet is distinct from the Amos in Luke's family list.

record.name: Amaziah the priest of Bethel
record.summary: Bethel's priest, distinct from the king of Judah with the same name. In Amos 7, he tells Jeroboam that Amos is plotting against him and the land cannot bear his words. He reports a prediction of Jeroboam's violent death and Israel's captivity. Calling Amos “O thou seer”, he tells him to leave for Judah and earn his living by speaking there. He orders him to stop speaking at Bethel because it is the king's chapel and court.

record.name: Eliphaz
record.summary: Called the Temanite, he is one of Job's three friends. They agree to visit, mourn and comfort Job, and Eliphaz speaks first. At the close, the story describes the Lord rebuking him and the other two friends for their words about God. They are told to offer bulls and rams while Job prays for them. Genesis 36 names an Eliphaz in Esau's family; Job does not identify its speaker as that man.

residence: Came to Job in his affliction (Job 2:11)

record.name: Bildad
record.summary: Called the Shuhite, he visits Job with Eliphaz and Zophar to mourn and comfort him. He speaks after Eliphaz. His arguments are his own speeches, not this profile's explanation of suffering. At the close, the story includes him in the Lord's rebuke of the three friends' words about God. He joins the others in making an offering while Job prays. The name Shuhite is retained without a further claim about his origin.

residence: Came to Job in his affliction (Job 2:11)

record.name: Zophar
record.summary: Called the Naamathite, he agrees to visit Job with the other two friends and speaks in turn. His arguments remain his own speeches, not this profile's explanation of suffering. At the close, the story includes him in the Lord's rebuke. He joins the others in offering seven bulls and seven rams while Job prays. No further fate is supplied here.

residence: Came to Job in his affliction (Job 2:11)

record.name: Elihu
record.summary: Barachel's son, called a Buzite from Ram's family. Job 32 says he waits for the older speakers to finish. It describes his anger at Job for defending himself rather than God. He is also angry at the three friends for condemning Job without finding an answer. He speaks in chapters 32–37 and says he too is made of clay. The Lord's later rebuke does not name him. Job 2:11 describes the three friends' visit, not Elihu's journey or home.

residence: Not stated; he speaks to Job in Job 32:6.

record.name: Mary
record.summary: A virgin from Nazareth, engaged to Joseph of Nazareth. Luke describes Gabriel announcing that she will bear Jesus, and her reply, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord”. She visits her relative Elisabeth and sings a prayer praising God. Luke places Jesus' birth in Bethlehem, where Mary lays him in a feeding trough. She presents him in the temple and later finds him there among the teachers. John places her at Cana's wedding and the cross, where Jesus entrusts her to the disciple he loved. Acts names her among those gathered after Jesus' ascent.

linked_stories.title: The Birth of Jesus and the Magi
The Births of John and Jesus
Presentation and the Boy Jesus in the Temple
The First Disciples and the Wedding at Cana

record.name: Joseph of Nazareth
record.summary: A man from David's family, engaged to Mary. Matthew calls him just and says he plans a private separation after learning she is pregnant. It describes an angel telling him to marry her and name the child Jesus. Luke places him with Mary at Bethlehem for registration. Matthew describes dream warnings leading him to take the family to Egypt and later return to Nazareth. Luke includes him at the temple presentation and the Passover visit when Jesus is twelve. These accounts describe his household relationship with Jesus without establishing biological parentage. These passages do not describe his later life. The Gospels do not name him at the cross.

children: Jesus (household relationship; no biological parentage inferred)

geography.origin: Nazareth in Galilee, of the house of David (Luke 1:27)

linked_stories.title: The Birth of Jesus and the Magi
Flight to Egypt and Return to Nazareth
The Births of John and Jesus
Presentation and the Boy Jesus in the Temple

record.name: Elisabeth
record.summary: Zacharias's wife, whom Luke describes as righteous, childless and advanced in years. Luke calls her a daughter of Aaron, meaning a family line rather than an immediate father. After an announcement to Zacharias in the temple, she becomes pregnant and stays hidden for five months. When her relative Mary visits, Luke describes the child moving within her and Elisabeth being filled with the Holy Spirit. She blesses Mary as her Lord's mother. At her child's naming, she insists he be called John.

linked_stories.title: The Births of John and Jesus

record.name: Zacharias
record.summary: A priest from Abia's service group and Elisabeth's husband. Luke describes Gabriel telling him in the temple that Elisabeth will bear a son named John. Gabriel links Zacharias's loss of speech to his unbelief. On the eighth day, Zacharias writes, “His name is John”. His speech returns when the child is named, and he praises God. His speech describes a saving power raised in David's family. This profile does not settle the identity of the Zacharias in Matthew 23:35.

geography.origin: A priest of the course of Abia (Luke 1:5)

linked_stories.title: The Births of John and Jesus

record.name: John the Baptist
record.summary: Zacharias and Elisabeth's son. Luke places the announcement to Mary in Elisabeth's sixth month of pregnancy, without giving an exact interval between births. Matthew describes John preaching changed lives in Judaea's wilderness, wearing camel hair and eating locusts and wild honey. He baptizes people who confess their sins in the Jordan. Luke records advice to crowds, soldiers and tax collectors; Matthew describes his rebuke of Pharisees and Sadducees. He baptizes Jesus, and John records his statement that Jesus must increase while he decreases. After rebuking Herod over Herodias, he is imprisoned. He sends disciples to question Jesus before the account of his execution.

geography.origin: Hill country of Judaea, son of Zacharias and Elisabeth (Luke 1:39-40, 57-60)

linked_stories.title: The Baptism and Temptation of Jesus
John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesus
The Births of John and Jesus
The First Disciples and the Wedding at Cana

record.name: Herod the king
record.summary: King of Judaea when Matthew places Jesus' birth. “Great” is a conventional label, not his quoted KJV name. Visiting wise men ask about the newborn king, troubling Herod and Jerusalem. Religious leaders name Bethlehem, and he tells the visitors to report back. Matthew says their return by another road angers him. He orders the killing of children aged two and under in Bethlehem and nearby areas. After his death, Matthew describes Joseph bringing the family from Egypt. Luke places John's birth in his reign. He is distinct from Herod the tetrarch and the Herod in Acts known as Agrippa.

linked_stories.title: The Birth of Jesus and the Magi
Flight to Egypt and Return to Nazareth

record.name: Peter
record.summary: A fisherman from Bethsaida, Andrew's brother, called Simon and named Peter by Jesus. Luke describes him leaving his nets after an extraordinary catch. The Gospels' calling accounts are kept distinct here. Peter comes first in lists of the Twelve. Matthew describes him walking on water, sinking and declaring, “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God”. Jesus rebukes him for resisting the warning of his coming suffering and death. Peter sees Jesus transformed on the mountain and later promises not to deny him. After the arrest, he denies Jesus three times and weeps. John describes his tomb visit and the risen Jesus asking about his love and directing him to feed his sheep.

linked_stories.title: Breakfast by the Sea of Tiberias

record.name: Judas Iscariot
record.summary: One of the Twelve, named as Jesus' betrayer. John says he keeps the money bag and steals from it. His protest at the Bethany anointing lacks concern for the poor. Matthew describes his agreement with the priests for thirty silver pieces. At supper, he is identified as the betrayer. He later leads the arresting group and identifies Jesus with a kiss. Matthew says he repents, returns the silver and hangs himself. Acts gives a different death account; this profile does not combine them. The cited verses do not establish his birthplace.

record.name: Mary Magdalene
record.summary: A woman called Magdalene, from whom Luke says seven devils had gone. She travels with Jesus and supports him from her resources. The Gospels place her among the women at the cross and describe her seeing his burial place. She finds the tomb's stone moved at dawn. John describes her weeping there and Jesus calling her by name. John says she tells the disciples that she has seen the Lord. The Gospels do not identify her with Luke 7's unnamed woman or Mary of Bethany. Her birthplace is not stated in the cited passage.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; Luke calls her Magdalene (Luke 8:2).

record.name: Martha
record.summary: Mary and Lazarus's sister from Bethany in John. Luke 10 describes a Martha welcoming Jesus and asking him to make Mary help with serving. Its village is unnamed, so the cross-account identity remains qualified here. In John, Martha meets Jesus after Lazarus dies and says, “if thou hadst been here”. She declares him the Christ and God's Son. At the tomb, she objects that the body will smell. John later describes her serving at a meal six days before Passover.

residence: Bethany (John 11:1); Luke 10:38 leaves its village unnamed.

linked_stories.title: The Good Samaritan and Mary and Martha

record.name: Mary of Bethany
record.summary: Martha and Lazarus's sister from Bethany in John. Luke 10 describes a Mary hearing Jesus while Martha serves, but leaves the village unnamed. This profile keeps that cross-account identity qualified. In John, Mary remains home after Lazarus dies until she is called. She falls at Jesus' feet and says, “if thou hadst been here”. John describes Jesus weeping and raising Lazarus. Before Passover, Mary pours costly spikenard perfume on Jesus' feet and wipes them with her hair. Judas objects; Jesus links her act to his burial. Matthew and Mark leave their Bethany anointing woman unnamed. She is not identified here with Luke 7's unnamed woman.

linked_stories.title: The Good Samaritan and Mary and Martha

record.name: Lazarus
record.summary: Martha and Mary's brother from Bethany, whom John says Jesus loves. He becomes ill and dies, spending four days in the grave before Jesus arrives. John describes Jesus thanking the Father and calling, “Lazarus, come forth”. Lazarus emerges in burial cloths, and Jesus tells others to free him. Many believe because of this account's event. Before Passover, Lazarus eats with Jesus, and the chief priests plan to kill him too. This Lazarus is distinct from the character in Luke 16's story.

record.name: Nicodemus
record.summary: A Pharisee, a member of a Jewish religious group, and a leader who visits Jesus at night in John. He says Jesus' miracles show God is with him. Jesus speaks of being born again through water and the Spirit: a new birth Nicodemus struggles to understand. The dialogue turns to the raised serpent and God's love in John 3:16. In John 7, Nicodemus asks whether the law judges someone before hearing him. After the crucifixion, he brings about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes, substances used in preparing a body. He helps Joseph of Arimathaea bury Jesus.

geography.origin: A Pharisee, a ruler of the Jews (John 3:1)

record.name: Pontius Pilate
record.summary: The Roman governor of Judaea before whom Jesus appears after his arrest. The Gospels record him asking, “Art thou the King of the Jews?” and declaring no fault. Luke describes him sending Jesus to Herod. The accounts also describe the offer involving Barabbas; Matthew adds his wife's warning and his hand washing. He has Jesus whipped and hands him over for crucifixion. John gives the cross inscription as “Jesus Of Nazareth The King Of The Jews”. He grants Joseph of Arimathaea the body. Matthew describes a guard at the tomb. Luke 13:1 mentions Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices.

linked_stories.title: Trial, Crucifixion and Burial in Mark

record.name: Caiaphas
record.summary: The high priest in the year of Jesus' death. After Lazarus is raised, John records him saying it is better for one man to die for the people. John interprets those words through Caiaphas's role as high priest. Matthew describes leaders plotting Jesus' arrest in his palace. After Jesus is brought there, Caiaphas tears his clothes at Jesus' reply. John calls Annas his father-in-law. Luke names Annas and Caiaphas together as high priests. Acts includes Caiaphas among the rulers questioning Peter and John.

record.name: Zacchaeus
record.summary: A wealthy chief tax collector in Jericho. Luke says he is short and climbs a sycomore tree to see Jesus. Jesus calls him by name and says he must stay at his house. The crowd objects that Jesus is visiting a sinner. Zacchaeus says he gives half his goods to the poor and repays any false charges fourfold. Luke records Jesus saying salvation has come to the house. Jesus describes his mission as seeking and saving the lost.

record.name: Thomas
record.summary: One of the Twelve, called Didymus, meaning twin. In John, he urges the others to go with Jesus after Lazarus dies: “Let us also go, that we may die with him”. At supper, he asks about the way; Jesus replies, “I am the way, the truth, and the life”. He misses Jesus' first appearance to the gathered disciples after the resurrection. He says he will not believe without seeing the nail marks and touching Jesus' side. John describes another appearance eight days later, when Thomas answers, “My Lord and my God”. He is later present at the sea of Tiberias and named in the upper-room gathering.

geography.origin: Not stated; one of the Twelve (Matthew 10:3)

linked_stories.title: Breakfast by the Sea of Tiberias

record.name: Stephen
record.summary: One of seven chosen in Acts to help distribute food to widows among Greek-speaking disciples. The language description does not assign a modern nationality. Acts describes him as full of faith, the Holy Spirit and power, and doing wonders. Men from several synagogues dispute with him and accuse him of speaking against the temple and law. His defence retells Israel's history and accuses his hearers of resisting the Holy Spirit. Acts describes him seeing Jesus at God's right hand. He is stoned outside the city while praying, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit”, and asking forgiveness for his attackers. Saul approves his death.

record.name: Barnabas
record.summary: Joses, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles call Barnabas. Acts 4:36 explains the name as “The son of consolation”, or encouragement. He sells land and gives the money to the apostles. He introduces Saul to the apostles and supports his account of preaching in Damascus. Sent to Antioch, he welcomes what Acts calls God's grace. Acts praises his character, faith and fullness of the Holy Spirit. He brings Saul from Tarsus, and Antioch's church sends them on a journey. Later, he wants John Mark to join them. A sharp dispute with Paul separates them; Barnabas sails to Cyprus with Mark.

record.name: Philip the evangelist
record.summary: One of the seven chosen with Stephen at Jerusalem. After the persecution following Stephen's death, Acts describes Philip preaching Christ in Samaria, where men and women are baptized. An angel directs him toward Gaza. He meets an Ethiopian officer reading Isaiah, explains the passage and baptizes him. Acts then describes Philip being carried away and found at Azotus. He preaches along the coast to Caesarea. Years later, Paul's group stays at his home there, where he has four unmarried daughters who prophesy. This profile is separate from Philip the apostle.

record.name: Cornelius
record.summary: A Roman officer in the Italian unit at Caesarea. Acts describes him and his household as devoted to God, with Cornelius giving to the poor and praying often. It describes an angel telling him to send for Peter at Joppa while Peter has a vision. Cornelius gathers relatives and close friends. Acts says the Holy Spirit comes upon those listening to Peter. Peter directs their baptism and stays at their request. Later, Peter explains the visit in Jerusalem. In Acts 11:18, his listeners conclude that God has granted life-giving repentance to non-Jews.

record.name: Silas
record.summary: A leader in Jerusalem's church, sent with Judas Barsabas to bring its council's letter to Antioch. Acts describes him as a prophet who encourages the believers. After Paul's dispute with Barnabas, Paul chooses Silas as a companion. At Philippi, they are beaten and jailed. Acts describes them praying and singing at midnight before an earthquake. Silas stays with Timothy at Berea and later rejoins Paul at Corinth. Letters name Silvanus with Paul and Timothy and mention his preaching among the Corinthians. The proposed Silas/Silvanus link remains qualified; the name forms alone do not prove it.

record.name: Timothy
record.summary: A disciple whom Acts introduces at Lystra, without stating his birthplace. His mother is a Jewish believer and his father is Greek. Local believers speak well of him. Paul takes him along and circumcises him because of the Jews in that region. He stays with Silas at Berea, rejoins Paul at Corinth and travels into Asia. Paul's letters call him his son in faith and recall the faith of Lois, his grandmother, and Eunice, his mother. First Timothy 1:3 places him at Ephesus. His father's name is not supplied here.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; Acts 16:1 introduces him at Lystra.

record.name: Apollos
record.summary: A Jew born in Alexandria, described in Acts as a skilled speaker with strong knowledge of scripture. He teaches in Ephesus while knowing only John's baptism. Aquila and Priscilla explain God's way to him more fully. With letters from the believers, he goes to Achaia and helps those who believe. In First Corinthians, Paul writes, “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase”. A later letter asks that Apollos and Zenas receive help for their journey. No claim about authorship of Hebrews is made here.

record.name: Priscilla
record.summary: Aquila's wife, who leaves Italy with him after Claudius orders Jews to leave Rome. Acts 18:2 names Aquila as Jewish without expressly saying this about Priscilla. At Corinth, they welcome Paul and work with him making tents. They travel with Paul to Ephesus, where they explain God's way more fully to Apollos. Paul calls them his helpers, and a church meets in their house. Her name appears before or after Aquila's in different passages. Second Timothy 4:19 uses Prisca.

geography.origin: Not stated; recently come from Italy (Acts 18:2)

record.name: Aquila
record.summary: A Jew born in Pontus, who arrives from Italy with Priscilla after Claudius's decree. Acts says he shares Paul's trade, and they make tents together at Corinth. He travels with Paul to Ephesus and joins Priscilla in teaching Apollos. Paul calls the pair his helpers and sends greetings “with the church that is in their house”. These passages do not give the date or circumstances of their conversion.

record.name: Gamaliel
record.summary: A Pharisee and law teacher whom Acts describes as widely respected. During the apostles' trial, he asks that they leave briefly and warns the council to act carefully. He argues that a human movement will fail, while a movement from God cannot be overthrown. Opposing it could mean fighting God. The council agrees, but has the apostles beaten and forbids speaking in Jesus' name. Paul later says Gamaliel taught him. Acts does not say this advice means Gamaliel joined the movement. He is distinct from the Gamaliel in Numbers.

linked_stories.title: The Lame Man Healed and Arrest of Peter and John

record.name: Lydia
record.summary: A seller of purple goods from Thyatira who worships God. She hears Paul at a riverside prayer gathering outside Philippi. Acts says the Lord opens her heart to his words. She and her household are baptized, and she urges Paul's group to stay at her house. After prison, Paul and Silas return there to meet and comfort the believers. The account does not state her marital status, wealth or household members' ages.

record.name: Felix
record.summary: The Roman governor to whom Paul is sent under guard from Jerusalem to Caesarea. He hears the high priest's accusation and Paul's reply. Acts describes his knowledge of the movement and his delay until Lysias can come. He and his Jewish wife Drusilla hear Paul discuss faith in Christ. Paul speaks about right conduct, self-control and coming judgment. Felix becomes afraid and sends him away. Acts 24:26 also says he hopes Paul will offer money. Two years later, Festus replaces him. Acts says Felix leaves Paul imprisoned to please the Jewish leaders.

linked_stories.title: Paul Before Felix, Festus and Agrippa

record.name: Festus
record.summary: Porcius Festus, named in Acts 24:27 as Felix's successor. Three days after arriving, he visits Jerusalem. Leaders ask him to bring Paul there, while planning an ambush. Festus holds the hearing at Caesarea. Acts says he wishes to please the leaders when he asks Paul about a Jerusalem trial. Paul appeals to Caesar. After consulting his council, Festus grants the appeal. He later presents the case to visiting King Agrippa so he can decide what to write.

linked_stories.title: Paul Before Felix, Festus and Agrippa

record.name: Agrippa
record.summary: A king whom Acts calls Agrippa, visiting Caesarea with Bernice to greet Festus. He allows Paul to speak. Paul describes his earlier life as a Pharisee, persecution of the church and vision near Damascus. Paul asks, “King Agrippa, believest thou the prophets? I know that thou believest”. Agrippa replies, “Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian”. He and Festus agree that Paul has done nothing deserving death or imprisonment. Agrippa says Paul could have been freed without his appeal to Caesar. Acts does not give the fuller historical name Herod Agrippa II in this account.

linked_stories.title: Paul Before Felix, Festus and Agrippa

record.name: Andrew
record.summary: A fisherman from Bethsaida and Peter's brother. John first presents him as a follower of John the Baptist who brings Peter to Jesus. Matthew and Mark describe Jesus calling the brothers from their fishing nets. These scenes are not combined into one sequence here. Andrew points out the boy with five barley loaves before the feeding of the crowd. With Philip, he brings Greek visitors' request to Jesus. He is one of four who ask Jesus privately about the temple's future on the Mount of Olives.

linked_stories.title: The First Disciples and the Wedding at Cana

record.name: James son of Zebedee
record.summary: Zebedee's son, called with his brother John while they mend nets in their father's boat. They leave the boat and father to follow Jesus. Mark says Jesus names them Boanerges, sons of thunder. With Peter and John, James enters Jairus's house and sees Jesus transformed on the mountain. He and John ask for seats beside Jesus in glory, upsetting the other ten. Jesus says they will drink his cup. Luke describes them asking to call down fire after a Samaritan village refuses Jesus. Acts says King Herod kills James, John's brother, with a sword.

linked_stories.title: Peter's Confession and the Transfiguration in Mark

record.name: John son of Zebedee
record.summary: Zebedee's son and James's brother, called with James from their fishing boat. He joins Peter and James at Jairus's house and when Jesus is transformed on the mountain. He reports stopping a man who casts out devils in Jesus' name. With James, he requests seats beside Jesus and proposes fire against a Samaritan village. Acts places him with Peter at the temple, before the council and in Samaria. The council calls them “unlearned and ignorant men”. John's Gospel leaves the beloved disciple unnamed while saying that disciple testified and wrote these things. This profile does not identify that disciple as John or settle authorship.

linked_stories.title: Peter's Confession and the Transfiguration in Mark
The Lame Man Healed and Arrest of Peter and John

record.name: Matthew
record.summary: Matthew describes Jesus calling a tax collector named Matthew with “Follow me”, after which he follows. Mark describes a similar call to Levi, Alphaeus's son, while Luke names Levi. Luke says Levi leaves everything and holds a feast with tax collectors and others. Mark also places the meal at Levi's house. Matthew 10:3 names “Matthew the publican” among the Twelve; Acts includes Matthew in the upper room. The Matthew/Levi association is kept qualified here because no cited verse directly states it. Alphaeus is therefore not entered as Matthew's unqualified parent.

geography.origin: Not stated; at the receipt of custom (Matthew 9:9)

record.name: Philip the apostle
record.summary: A man from Bethsaida, also home to Andrew and Peter. John describes Jesus finding him in Galilee and saying, “Follow me”. He tells Nathanael they have found the figure Moses and the prophets wrote about. When Nathanael questions Nazareth, Philip replies, “Come and see”. Before the crowd is fed, he says two hundred pennyworth of bread would not be enough. Greek visitors approach him; he and Andrew bring their request to Jesus. At supper, he asks to see the Father. Jesus replies that seeing him means seeing the Father. Acts names him in the upper room. He is distinct from Philip the evangelist.

linked_stories.title: The First Disciples and the Wedding at Cana

record.name: Nathanael
record.summary: Philip brings him to Jesus after saying they have found the figure described in the law and prophets. Nathanael questions whether good can come from Nazareth. John describes Jesus greeting him as an Israelite without deceit and saying he saw him under the fig tree. Nathanael replies, “Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel.” John 21:2 calls him “of Cana in Galilee” among the disciples at the sea of Tiberias. The cited passages do not call him an apostle or identify him with Bartholomew.

linked_stories.title: The First Disciples and the Wedding at Cana
Breakfast by the Sea of Tiberias

record.name: Herod the tetrarch
record.summary: Called Herod the tetrarch, ruling Galilee in Tiberius's fifteenth year. Antipas is a conventional historical label, not the KJV name. John rebukes his marriage to Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, and Herod imprisons him. Mark says Herod fears John and listens gladly. At a birthday feast, he promises Herodias's daughter whatever she asks. Though sorry, he orders John's execution to keep his oath. Hearing about Jesus, he says John has risen. Luke records a warning that Herod seeks Jesus' death and Jesus calling him a fox. At trial, Herod questions and mocks Jesus, then returns him to Pilate. Luke says the two rulers become friends that day.

geography.origin: Not stated in the Gospels; tetrarch of Galilee (Luke 3:1)
residence: Jerusalem at the time of the trial (Luke 23:7)

linked_stories.title: Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on Water

record.name: Herodias
record.summary: Herod the tetrarch's wife, described in the Gospels as previously married to his brother Philip. John tells Herod that this marriage is unlawful. Mark says Herodias wants John killed but cannot while Herod protects him. At Herod's birthday feast, her daughter dances and receives a promise of whatever she requests. Herodias tells her to ask for John's head. The daughter brings it to her mother on a platter. The Gospels leave the daughter unnamed; no fuller family tree is added here.

linked_stories.title: Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on Water

record.name: Joseph of Arimathaea
record.summary: A man from Arimathaea, distinct from Mary's husband and the patriarch Joseph. Matthew calls him rich; John describes him as a secret disciple who fears the Jewish leaders. Mark calls him a respected council member awaiting God's kingdom. Luke says he did not agree with the council's actions. Mark describes him boldly asking Pilate for Jesus' body, which Pilate grants after checking that Jesus is dead. Matthew says he wraps it in clean linen and places it in his own new rock-cut tomb. John describes Nicodemus bringing myrrh and aloes and both men wrapping the body with these substances.

geography.origin: Arimathaea (Matthew 27:57; Luke 23:51 'a city of the Jews')

linked_stories.title: Trial, Crucifixion and Burial in Mark

record.name: Barabbas
record.summary: A prisoner offered for release during the feast. Matthew calls him notable. Mark links him with rebels who committed murder; Luke names revolt and murder; John calls him a robber. These descriptions remain attributed to their Gospels and do not establish different identities. Matthew describes the priests urging the crowd to choose Barabbas and demand Jesus' death. Pilate asks what wrong Jesus has done, then releases Barabbas and hands Jesus over for crucifixion. The accounts give no later biography for Barabbas.

linked_stories.title: Trial, Crucifixion and Burial in Mark

record.name: Annas
record.summary: Named with Caiaphas as high priest in Luke when John begins receiving God's word. John says Jesus is first brought to Annas, Caiaphas's father-in-law, after his arrest. It then describes “the high priest” questioning Jesus about his followers and teaching. Jesus says he spoke openly, and an officer strikes him. John says Annas sent Jesus bound to Caiaphas. The passage names both men without settling the questioner's identity here. Acts again calls Annas high priest when Peter and John face the rulers. Caiaphas, John, Alexander and others from the high priest's family are also present.

record.name: Ananias
record.summary: A Jerusalem believer whose wife is Sapphira, distinct from the Damascus disciple and the high priest named Ananias. Acts says the couple sell property and knowingly keep part of the price while bringing the rest to the apostles. Peter says both land and money had been theirs to use freely. He accuses Ananias of lying to God. The account says Ananias falls down dead and fear spreads among those who hear. Young men wrap and bury him.

residence: Jerusalem (implied by Acts 5:1-2, the apostles' feet)

record.name: Sapphira
record.summary: Ananias's wife, who knows about the plan to keep part of the land's price. Acts says she comes in about three hours later, unaware of what has happened. Peter separately asks her whether the land sold for the stated amount, and she says yes. He asks why they agreed to test the Lord's Spirit. He says the men who buried her husband are at the door. Acts describes her falling dead at Peter's feet and being buried beside her husband.

record.name: Ananias of Damascus
aliases: Ananias, a devout man according to the law
record.summary: A disciple at Damascus, distinct from Sapphira's husband and the high priest. Acts 9 describes the Lord sending him in a vision to Judas's house on Straight Street. Saul is praying there and has seen Ananias coming to lay a hand on him. Ananias objects, citing Saul's persecution and authority to arrest believers. The Lord's reply describes Saul as chosen to speak before non-Jews, kings and Israel. Ananias goes, lays hands on Saul and calls him brother. He says he was sent for Saul's sight and filling with the Holy Spirit. In Paul's later account, Ananias follows the law and is respected by local Jews.

record.name: Simon the sorcerer
record.summary: A man in Samaria whom Acts describes as using sorcery and presenting himself as great. People call him God's great power. After Philip preaches, Simon believes, is baptized and follows him, amazed by the signs. Acts describes Peter and John laying hands on people, who receive the Holy Spirit. Simon offers money for that power. Peter rebukes him and tells him to turn from his wrongdoing and pray. Simon asks them to pray that the threatened harm will not happen. Acts gives no later biography. Magus is a conventional label, not his name in the KJV; he is distinct from Peter and Simon the tanner.

record.name: Dorcas
record.summary: Tabitha, also called Dorcas, is a disciple in Joppa whom Acts describes as generous and active in helping others. She becomes ill, dies and is laid in an upstairs room. Two men ask Peter to come from nearby Lydda. Widows show him clothing she made and weep. Acts describes Peter clearing the room, kneeling to pray and saying, “Tabitha, arise”. She opens her eyes and sits up, and he presents her alive to the believers and widows. The account says many in Joppa believe after hearing this.

record.name: Eutychus
record.summary: A young man present at Troas, sitting in an upstairs window while Paul speaks until midnight before leaving. Acts says he falls deeply asleep, falls from the third floor and is taken up dead. Paul goes down, embraces him and says his life is in him. Paul returns upstairs, breaks bread and talks until dawn. The account describes Eutychus being brought in alive, greatly comforting the group. It does not establish his beliefs from attendance or explain a medical mechanism.

record.name: Demetrius the silversmith
record.summary: A silversmith in Ephesus who makes silver shrines for Diana. Acts records him warning other craftspeople that Paul's teaching threatens their income and the goddess's temple. He says Paul teaches that handmade gods are not gods. The workers shout, “Great is Diana of the Ephesians”, and confusion spreads through the city. The town clerk calms the crowd. He says the accused men neither rob temples nor insult their goddess, and directs complaints to the courts. This profile covers the silversmith in Acts, without identifying him with the Demetrius in 3 John.

record.name: Claudius Lysias
record.summary: The Roman commander at Jerusalem, distinct from Emperor Claudius. Acts describes him rescuing Paul from a crowd and binding him with two chains. He asks whether Paul is the Egyptian rebel; Paul replies that he is a Jew from Tarsus. The officer orders a whipping to question Paul but draws back on learning Paul is Roman. He says he bought citizenship, while Paul says he was born with it. After Paul's nephew reports an ambush plot, he sends Paul to Felix at Caesarea under a large guard. His letter names him and says Paul has done nothing deserving death or imprisonment. Those assessments remain the officer's claims.

geography.origin: Not stated; he bought Roman citizenship (Acts 22:28)

record.name: Luke
record.summary: Paul's companion named in three letters. Philemon calls Lucas a fellow worker; Colossians calls Luke “the beloved physician”; Second Timothy says only Luke is with Paul. The last passage does not establish a final imprisonment. Acts never names Luke, though its narration changes to “we” in parts of the journeys. Acts addresses Theophilus and refers to “The former treatise”; Luke's Gospel also addresses Theophilus. The traditional link between these books, Luke and the unnamed travelling narrator is not an explicit statement of the texts.

residence: Not stated in the cited letters.

record.title: Jehu paying tribute to Shalmaneser III (Black Obelisk)
record.traditional_date: Reported tribute in Shalmaneser III's eighteenth year, usually dated to c. 841 BCE.
record.review_status: Context only. Assyrian texts report tribute absent from the compared Kings account.
record.display_title: Jehu Paying Tribute to Shalmaneser III (Black Obelisk)

record.title: Esarhaddon and Manasseh of Judah
record.traditional_date: Manasseh's reign; the text gives fifty-five years. Esarhaddon's reign is usually dated to 680–669 BCE.
record.review_status: Context only. The palace-building list names Manasseh; the biblical accounts report different details of his reign.

record.title: Merodach-baladan and Hezekiah
record.traditional_date: Hezekiah's reign, during the reign setting of Merodach-baladan. The embassy's year is not fixed here.
record.review_status: Context only. The chronicle records the Babylonian king's reign, not this embassy.

record.title: Nebuchadnezzar's campaign against Egypt (567 BCE)
record.traditional_date: Nebuchadnezzar's thirty-seventh year: c. 568/567 BCE. Ezekiel 29:17 dates its message to the twenty-seventh year.
record.review_status: Context only. A damaged campaign notice is compared with predictions; it does not settle the outcome.

record.traditional_date: During the famine in Genesis 12; no year fixed by outside sources
record.review_status: needs review: passage order checked; outside dates not checked

sourceReview.scope: The episode follows Abram’s arrival in Canaan. Similar scenes in other chapters do not establish one shared event.
sourceReview.review_method: The KJV narrative placement and existing evidence pointer were checked. The linked record’s other source claims were not re-audited.

quote_checks.quote: Now the Lord had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:
And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing:
And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.
So Abram departed, as the Lord had spoken unto him; and Lot went with him: and Abram was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran.

And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their substance that they had gathered, and the souls that they had gotten in Haran; and they went forth to go into the land of Canaan; and into the land of Canaan they came.
And Abram passed through the land unto the place of Sichem, unto the plain of Moreh. And the Canaanite was then in the land.
And the Lord appeared unto Abram, and said, Unto thy seed will I give this land: and there builded he an altar unto the Lord, who appeared unto him.

And he removed from thence unto a mountain on the east of Bethel, and pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west, and Hai on the east: and there he builded an altar unto the Lord, and called upon the name of the Lord.
And Abram journeyed, going on still toward the south.
And there was a famine in the land: and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there; for the famine was grievous in the land.
And it came to pass, when he was come near to enter into Egypt, that he said unto Sarai his wife, Behold now, I know that thou art a fair woman to look upon:
Therefore it shall come to pass, when the Egyptians shall see thee, that they shall say, This is his wife: and they will kill me, but they will save thee alive.
Say, I pray thee, thou art my sister: that it may be well with me for thy sake; and my soul shall live because of thee.
And it came to pass, that, when Abram was come into Egypt, the Egyptians beheld the woman that she was very fair.
The princes also of Pharaoh saw her, and commended her before Pharaoh: and the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house.
And he entreated Abram well for her sake: and he had sheep, and oxen, and he asses, and menservants, and maidservants, and she asses, and camels.
And the Lord plagued Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai Abram's wife.
And Pharaoh called Abram and said, What is this that thou hast done unto me? why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife?
Why saidst thou, She is my sister? so I might have taken her to me to wife: now therefore behold thy wife, take her, and go thy way.
And Pharaoh commanded his men concerning him: and they sent him away, and his wife, and all that he had.

record.title: Abraham And Sarah At Gerar
record.traditional_date: Before Isaac’s birth in Genesis 21; no year fixed by outside sources
record.review_status: needs review: passage order checked; outside dates not checked

sourceReview.scope: This is the order of the Genesis narrative. The review does not assign a date to the ruler named Abimelech.
sourceReview.review_method: The KJV narrative placement and existing evidence pointer were checked. The linked record’s other source claims were not re-audited.

quote_checks.quote: And Abraham journeyed from thence toward the south country, and dwelled between Kadesh and Shur, and sojourned in Gerar.
And Abraham said of Sarah his wife, She is my sister: and Abimelech king of Gerar sent, and took Sarah.
But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night, and said to him, Behold, thou art but a dead man, for the woman which thou hast taken; for she is a man's wife.
But Abimelech had not come near her: and he said, Lord, wilt thou slay also a righteous nation?
Said he not unto me, She is my sister? and she, even she herself said, He is my brother: in the integrity of my heart and innocency of my hands have I done this.
And God said unto him in a dream, Yea, I know that thou didst this in the integrity of thy heart; for I also withheld thee from sinning against me: therefore suffered I thee not to touch her.

Now therefore restore the man his wife; for he is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee, and thou shalt live: and if thou restore her not, know thou that thou shalt surely die, thou, and all that are thine.
Therefore Abimelech rose early in the morning, and called all his servants, and told all these things in their ears: and the men were sore afraid.

Then Abimelech called Abraham, and said unto him, What hast thou done unto us? and what have I offended thee, that thou hast brought on me and on my kingdom a great sin? thou hast done deeds unto me that ought not to be done.
And Abimelech said unto Abraham, What sawest thou, that thou hast done this thing?
And Abraham said, Because I thought, Surely the fear of God is not in this place; and they will slay me for my wife's sake.
And yet indeed she is my sister; she is the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother; and she became my wife.

And it came to pass, when God caused me to wander from my father's house, that I said unto her, This is thy kindness which thou shalt shew unto me; at every place whither we shall come, say of me, He is my brother.
And Abimelech took sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and womenservants, and gave them unto Abraham, and restored him Sarah his wife.
And Abimelech said, Behold, my land is before thee: dwell where it pleaseth thee.

And unto Sarah he said, Behold, I have given thy brother a thousand pieces of silver: behold, he is to thee a covering of the eyes, unto all that are with thee, and with all other: thus she was reproved.
So Abraham prayed unto God: and God healed Abimelech, and his wife, and his maidservants; and they bare children.
For the Lord had fast closed up all the wombs of the house of Abimelech, because of Sarah Abraham's wife.

record.title: Isaac And Rebekah At Gerar
record.traditional_date: During the famine described in Genesis 26; no year fixed by outside sources
record.review_status: needs review: passage order checked; outside dates not checked

sourceReview.scope: Genesis distinguishes this famine from the earlier one. The shared setting does not by itself identify the same ruler.
sourceReview.review_method: The KJV narrative placement and existing evidence pointer were checked. The linked record’s other source claims were not re-audited.

quote_checks.quote: And there was a famine in the land, beside the first famine that was in the days of Abraham. And Isaac went unto Abimelech king of the Philistines unto Gerar.
And the Lord appeared unto him, and said, Go not down into Egypt; dwell in the land which I shall tell thee of:

Sojourn in this land, and I will be with thee, and will bless thee; for unto thee, and unto thy seed, I will give all these countries, and I will perform the oath which I sware unto Abraham thy father;
And I will make thy seed to multiply as the stars of heaven, and will give unto thy seed all these countries; and in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed;
Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.
And Isaac dwelt in Gerar:

And the men of the place asked him of his wife; and he said, She is my sister: for he feared to say, She is my wife; lest, said he, the men of the place should kill me for Rebekah; because she was fair to look upon.
And it came to pass, when he had been there a long time, that Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out at a window, and saw, and, behold, Isaac was sporting with Rebekah his wife.
And Abimelech called Isaac, and said, Behold, of a surety she is thy wife; and how saidst thou, She is my sister? And Isaac said unto him, Because I said, Lest I die for her.
And Abimelech said, What is this thou hast done unto us? one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us.
And Abimelech charged all his people, saying, He that toucheth this man or his wife shall surely be put to death.
Then Isaac sowed in that land, and received in the same year an hundredfold: and the Lord blessed him.
And the man waxed great, and went forward, and grew until he became very great:
For he had possession of flocks, and possession of herds, and great store of servants: and the Philistines envied him.
For all the wells which his father's servants had digged in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped them, and filled them with earth.
And Abimelech said unto Isaac, Go from us; for thou art much mightier than we.
And Isaac departed thence, and pitched his tent in the valley of Gerar, and dwelt there.

And Isaac digged again the wells of water, which they had digged in the days of Abraham his father; for the Philistines had stopped them after the death of Abraham: and he called their names after the names by which his father had called them.
And Isaac's servants digged in the valley, and found there a well of springing water.
And the herdmen of Gerar did strive with Isaac's herdmen, saying, The water is ours: and he called the name of the well Esek; because they strove with him.

And Moses told Aaron all the words of the Lord who had sent him, and all the signs which he had commanded him.
And Moses and Aaron went and gathered together all the elders of the children of Israel:
And Aaron spake all the words which the Lord had spoken unto Moses, and did the signs in the sight of the people.
And the people believed: and when they heard that the Lord had visited the children of Israel, and that he had looked upon their affliction, then they bowed their heads and worshipped.
And afterward Moses and Aaron went in, and told Pharaoh, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Let my people go, that they may hold a feast unto me in the wilderness.
And Pharaoh said, Who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go? I know not the Lord, neither will I let Israel go.

And they said, The God of the Hebrews hath met with us: let us go, we pray thee, three days' journey into the desert, and sacrifice unto the Lord our God; lest he fall upon us with pestilence, or with the sword.
And the king of Egypt said unto them, Wherefore do ye, Moses and Aaron, let the people from their works? get you unto your burdens.
And Pharaoh said, Behold, the people of the land now are many, and ye make them rest from their burdens.
And Pharaoh commanded the same day the taskmasters of the people, and their officers, saying,
Ye shall no more give the people straw to make brick, as heretofore: let them go and gather straw for themselves.

And the tale of the bricks, which they did make heretofore, ye shall lay upon them; ye shall not diminish ought thereof: for they be idle; therefore they cry, saying, Let us go and sacrifice to our God.
Let there more work be laid upon the men, that they may labour therein; and let them not regard vain words.
And the taskmasters of the people went out, and their officers, and they spake to the people, saying, Thus saith Pharaoh, I will not give you straw.
Go ye, get you straw where ye can find it: yet not ought of your work shall be diminished.
So the people were scattered abroad throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble instead of straw.
And the taskmasters hasted them, saying, Fulfil your works, your daily tasks, as when there was straw.

And the officers of the children of Israel, which Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten, and demanded, Wherefore have ye not fulfilled your task in making brick both yesterday and to day, as heretofore?
Then the officers of the children of Israel came and cried unto Pharaoh, saying, Wherefore dealest thou thus with thy servants?
There is no straw given unto thy servants, and they say to us, Make brick: and, behold, thy servants are beaten; but the fault is in thine own people.
But he said, Ye are idle, ye are idle: therefore ye say, Let us go and do sacrifice to the Lord.
Go therefore now, and work; for there shall no straw be given you, yet shall ye deliver the tale of bricks.
And the officers of the children of Israel did see that they were in evil case, after it was said, Ye shall not minish ought from your bricks of your daily task.
And they met Moses and Aaron, who stood in the way, as they came forth from Pharaoh:

And they said unto them, The Lord look upon you, and judge; because ye have made our savour to be abhorred in the eyes of Pharaoh, and in the eyes of his servants, to put a sword in their hand to slay us.
And Moses returned unto the Lord, and said, Lord, wherefore hast thou so evil entreated this people? why is it that thou hast sent me?
For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in thy name, he hath done evil to this people; neither hast thou delivered thy people at all.
Then the Lord said unto Moses, Now shalt thou see what I will do to Pharaoh: for with a strong hand shall he let them go, and with a strong hand shall he drive them out of his land.
And God spake unto Moses, and said unto him, I am the Lord:
And I appeared unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, by the name of God Almighty, but by my name Jehovah was I not known to them.
And I have also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land of their pilgrimage, wherein they were strangers.
And I have also heard the groaning of the children of Israel, whom the Egyptians keep in bondage; and I have remembered my covenant.

Wherefore say unto the children of Israel, I am the Lord, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with a stretched out arm, and with great judgments:
And I will take you to me for a people, and I will be to you a God: and ye shall know that I am the Lord your God, which bringeth you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.
And I will bring you in unto the land, concerning the which I did swear to give it to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob; and I will give it you for an heritage: I am the Lord.
And Moses spake so unto the children of Israel: but they hearkened not unto Moses for anguish of spirit, and for cruel bondage.
And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying,
Go in, speak unto Pharaoh king of Egypt, that he let the children of Israel go out of his land.
And Moses spake before the Lord, saying, Behold, the children of Israel have not hearkened unto me; how then shall Pharaoh hear me, who am of uncircumcised lips?
And the Lord spake unto Moses and unto Aaron, and gave them a charge unto the children of Israel, and unto Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt.
These be the heads of their fathers' houses: The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel; Hanoch, and Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi: these be the families of Reuben.
And the sons of Simeon; Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad, and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanitish woman: these are the families of Simeon.
And these are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations; Gershon, and Kohath, and Merari: and the years of the life of Levi were an hundred thirty and seven years.
The sons of Gershon; Libni, and Shimi, according to their families.
And the sons of Kohath; Amram, and Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel: and the years of the life of Kohath were an hundred thirty and three years.
And the sons of Merari; Mahali and Mushi: these are the families of Levi according to their generations.
And Amram took him Jochebed his father's sister to wife; and she bare him Aaron and Moses: and the years of the life of Amram were an hundred and thirty and seven years.
And the sons of Izhar; Korah, and Nepheg, and Zichri.
And the sons of Uzziel; Mishael, and Elzaphan, and Zithri.
And Aaron took him Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Naashon, to wife; and she bare him Nadab, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
And the sons of Korah; Assir, and Elkanah, and Abiasaph: these are the families of the Korhites.
And Eleazar Aaron's son took him one of the daughters of Putiel to wife; and she bare him Phinehas: these are the heads of the fathers of the Levites according to their families.
These are that Aaron and Moses, to whom the Lord said, Bring out the children of Israel from the land of Egypt according to their armies.
These are they which spake to Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring out the children of Israel from Egypt: these are that Moses and Aaron.
And it came to pass on the day when the Lord spake unto Moses in the land of Egypt,
That the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, I am the Lord: speak thou unto Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say unto thee.
And Moses said before the Lord, Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips, and how shall Pharaoh hearken unto me?

quote_checks.quote: And the Lord said unto Moses, See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh: and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet.
Thou shalt speak all that I command thee: and Aaron thy brother shall speak unto Pharaoh, that he send the children of Israel out of his land.
And I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.
But Pharaoh shall not hearken unto you, that I may lay my hand upon Egypt, and bring forth mine armies, and my people the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great judgments.
And the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord, when I stretch forth mine hand upon Egypt, and bring out the children of Israel from among them.
And Moses and Aaron did as the Lord commanded them, so did they.
And Moses was fourscore years old, and Aaron fourscore and three years old, when they spake unto Pharaoh.
And the Lord spake unto Moses and unto Aaron, saying,
When Pharaoh shall speak unto you, saying, Shew a miracle for you: then thou shalt say unto Aaron, Take thy rod, and cast it before Pharaoh, and it shall become a serpent.
And Moses and Aaron went in unto Pharaoh, and they did so as the Lord had commanded: and Aaron cast down his rod before Pharaoh, and before his servants, and it became a serpent.
Then Pharaoh also called the wise men and the sorcerers: now the magicians of Egypt, they also did in like manner with their enchantments.
For they cast down every man his rod, and they became serpents: but Aaron's rod swallowed up their rods.
And he hardened Pharaoh's heart, that he hearkened not unto them; as the Lord had said.
And the Lord said unto Moses, Pharaoh's heart is hardened, he refuseth to let the people go.

Get thee unto Pharaoh in the morning; lo, he goeth out unto the water; and thou shalt stand by the river's brink against he come; and the rod which was turned to a serpent shalt thou take in thine hand.
And thou shalt say unto him, The Lord God of the Hebrews hath sent me unto thee, saying, Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness: and, behold, hitherto thou wouldest not hear.
Thus saith the Lord, In this thou shalt know that I am the Lord: behold, I will smite with the rod that is in mine hand upon the waters which are in the river, and they shall be turned to blood.
And the fish that is in the river shall die, and the river shall stink; and the Egyptians shall lothe to drink of the water of the river.

And the Lord spake unto Moses, Say unto Aaron, Take thy rod, and stretch out thine hand upon the waters of Egypt, upon their streams, upon their rivers, and upon their ponds, and upon all their pools of water, that they may become blood; and that there may be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, both in vessels of wood, and in vessels of stone.

And Moses and Aaron did so, as the Lord commanded; and he lifted up the rod, and smote the waters that were in the river, in the sight of Pharaoh, and in the sight of his servants; and all the waters that were in the river were turned to blood.
And the fish that was in the river died; and the river stank, and the Egyptians could not drink of the water of the river; and there was blood throughout all the land of Egypt.
And the magicians of Egypt did so with their enchantments: and Pharaoh's heart was hardened, neither did he hearken unto them; as the Lord had said.
And Pharaoh turned and went into his house, neither did he set his heart to this also.
And all the Egyptians digged round about the river for water to drink; for they could not drink of the water of the river.
And seven days were fulfilled, after that the Lord had smitten the river.
And the Lord spake unto Moses, Go unto Pharaoh, and say unto him, Thus saith the Lord, Let my people go, that they may serve me.
And if thou refuse to let them go, behold, I will smite all thy borders with frogs:

And the river shall bring forth frogs abundantly, which shall go up and come into thine house, and into thy bedchamber, and upon thy bed, and into the house of thy servants, and upon thy people, and into thine ovens, and into thy kneadingtroughs:
And the frogs shall come up both on thee, and upon thy people, and upon all thy servants.
And the Lord spake unto Moses, Say unto Aaron, Stretch forth thine hand with thy rod over the streams, over the rivers, and over the ponds, and cause frogs to come up upon the land of Egypt.
And Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt; and the frogs came up, and covered the land of Egypt.
And the magicians did so with their enchantments, and brought up frogs upon the land of Egypt.

Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron, and said, Intreat the Lord, that he may take away the frogs from me, and from my people; and I will let the people go, that they may do sacrifice unto the Lord.

And Moses said unto Pharaoh, Glory over me: when shall I intreat for thee, and for thy servants, and for thy people, to destroy the frogs from thee and thy houses, that they may remain in the river only?
And he said, To morrow. And he said, Be it according to thy word: that thou mayest know that there is none like unto the Lord our God.
And the frogs shall depart from thee, and from thy houses, and from thy servants, and from thy people; they shall remain in the river only.
And Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh: and Moses cried unto the Lord because of the frogs which he had brought against Pharaoh.
And the Lord did according to the word of Moses; and the frogs died out of the houses, out of the villages, and out of the fields.
And they gathered them together upon heaps: and the land stank.
But when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart, and hearkened not unto them; as the Lord had said.
And the Lord said unto Moses, Say unto Aaron, Stretch out thy rod, and smite the dust of the land, that it may become lice throughout all the land of Egypt.

And they did so; for Aaron stretched out his hand with his rod, and smote the dust of the earth, and it became lice in man, and in beast; all the dust of the land became lice throughout all the land of Egypt.
And the magicians did so with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not: so there were lice upon man, and upon beast.
Then the magicians said unto Pharaoh, This is the finger of God: and Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he hearkened not unto them; as the Lord had said.

And the Lord said unto Moses, Rise up early in the morning, and stand before Pharaoh; lo, he cometh forth to the water; and say unto him, Thus saith the Lord, Let my people go, that they may serve me.

Else, if thou wilt not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies upon thee, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people, and into thy houses: and the houses of the Egyptians shall be full of swarms of flies, and also the ground whereon they are.
And I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there; to the end thou mayest know that I am the Lord in the midst of the earth.
And I will put a division between my people and thy people: to morrow shall this sign be.

And the Lord did so; and there came a grievous swarm of flies into the house of Pharaoh, and into his servants' houses, and into all the land of Egypt: the land was corrupted by reason of the swarm of flies.
And Pharaoh called for Moses and for Aaron, and said, Go ye, sacrifice to your God in the land.

And Moses said, It is not meet so to do; for we shall sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians to the Lord our God: lo, shall we sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians before their eyes, and will they not stone us?
We will go three days' journey into the wilderness, and sacrifice to the Lord our God, as he shall command us.
And Pharaoh said, I will let you go, that ye may sacrifice to the Lord your God in the wilderness; only ye shall not go very far away: intreat for me.

And Moses said, Behold, I go out from thee, and I will intreat the Lord that the swarms of flies may depart from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people, to morrow: but let not Pharaoh deal deceitfully any more in not letting the people go to sacrifice to the Lord.
And Moses went out from Pharaoh, and intreated the Lord.
And the Lord did according to the word of Moses; and he removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people; there remained not one.
And Pharaoh hardened his heart at this time also, neither would he let the people go.
Then the Lord said unto Moses, Go in unto Pharaoh, and tell him, Thus saith the Lord God of the Hebrews, Let my people go, that they may serve me.
For if thou refuse to let them go, and wilt hold them still,
Behold, the hand of the Lord is upon thy cattle which is in the field, upon the horses, upon the asses, upon the camels, upon the oxen, and upon the sheep: there shall be a very grievous murrain.
And the Lord shall sever between the cattle of Israel and the cattle of Egypt: and there shall nothing die of all that is the children's of Israel.
And the Lord appointed a set time, saying, To morrow the Lord shall do this thing in the land.
And the Lord did that thing on the morrow, and all the cattle of Egypt died: but of the cattle of the children of Israel died not one.
And Pharaoh sent, and, behold, there was not one of the cattle of the Israelites dead. And the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people go.
And the Lord said unto Moses and unto Aaron, Take to you handfuls of ashes of the furnace, and let Moses sprinkle it toward the heaven in the sight of Pharaoh.
And it shall become small dust in all the land of Egypt, and shall be a boil breaking forth with blains upon man, and upon beast, throughout all the land of Egypt.
And they took ashes of the furnace, and stood before Pharaoh; and Moses sprinkled it up toward heaven; and it became a boil breaking forth with blains upon man, and upon beast.
And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils; for the boil was upon the magicians, and upon all the Egyptians.
And the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he hearkened not unto them; as the Lord had spoken unto Moses.
And the Lord said unto Moses, Rise up early in the morning, and stand before Pharaoh, and say unto him, Thus saith the Lord God of the Hebrews, Let my people go, that they may serve me.
For I will at this time send all my plagues upon thine heart, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people; that thou mayest know that there is none like me in all the earth.
For now I will stretch out my hand, that I may smite thee and thy people with pestilence; and thou shalt be cut off from the earth.
And in very deed for this cause have I raised thee up, for to shew in thee my power; and that my name may be declared throughout all the earth.
As yet exaltest thou thyself against my people, that thou wilt not let them go?
Behold, to morrow about this time I will cause it to rain a very grievous hail, such as hath not been in Egypt since the foundation thereof even until now.

Send therefore now, and gather thy cattle, and all that thou hast in the field; for upon every man and beast which shall be found in the field, and shall not be brought home, the hail shall come down upon them, and they shall die.
He that feared the word of the Lord among the servants of Pharaoh made his servants and his cattle flee into the houses:
And he that regarded not the word of the Lord left his servants and his cattle in the field.

And the Lord said unto Moses, Stretch forth thine hand toward heaven, that there may be hail in all the land of Egypt, upon man, and upon beast, and upon every herb of the field, throughout the land of Egypt.
And Moses stretched forth his rod toward heaven: and the Lord sent thunder and hail, and the fire ran along upon the ground; and the Lord rained hail upon the land of Egypt.
So there was hail, and fire mingled with the hail, very grievous, such as there was none like it in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation.
And the hail smote throughout all the land of Egypt all that was in the field, both man and beast; and the hail smote every herb of the field, and brake every tree of the field.
Only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, was there no hail.
And Pharaoh sent, and called for Moses and Aaron, and said unto them, I have sinned this time: the Lord is righteous, and I and my people are wicked.
Intreat the Lord (for it is enough) that there be no more mighty thunderings and hail; and I will let you go, and ye shall stay no longer.

And Moses said unto him, As soon as I am gone out of the city, I will spread abroad my hands unto the Lord; and the thunder shall cease, neither shall there be any more hail; that thou mayest know how that the earth is the Lord's.
But as for thee and thy servants, I know that ye will not yet fear the Lord God.
And the flax and the barley was smitten: for the barley was in the ear, and the flax was bolled.
But the wheat and the rie were not smitten: for they were not grown up.
And Moses went out of the city from Pharaoh, and spread abroad his hands unto the Lord: and the thunders and hail ceased, and the rain was not poured upon the earth.
And when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunders were ceased, he sinned yet more, and hardened his heart, he and his servants.
And the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, neither would he let the children of Israel go; as the Lord had spoken by Moses.
